reactors.name: ACP100 / Linglong One
reactors.fuel: UO2 pellets, 17x17 square-pitch assemblies; discharge burnup <52 GWd/t
reactors.fnote: Standard <4.95% LEU UO2 17x17 fuel supplied through CNNC's fully integrated domestic fuel cycle (mining, conversion, enrichment, fabrication at CJNF/Yibin). No fuel-supply risk inside China; for any export customer the fuel supply would be Chinese-sourced with the geopolitical dependency that implies.
reactors.tnote: Reactor pressure vessel is 10 m x 3.35 m and 300 t (IAEA ARIS) — heavy-lift/barge delivery to a coastal or major-river site only. Plant footprint 200,000 m2 per ARIS. Not a road-transportable microreactor.

lic.s: Construction permit issued; construction start 13 July 2021. Operating licence / fuel load authorisation pending.
First IAEA GRSR final safety review report ever issued for an SMR

reactors.cnote: NOT YET OPERATING as of 8 August 2026 — this is the single most commonly mis-stated fact about this design. IAEA PRIS (database updated 17 July 2026) still lists LINGLONG-1 as 'Under Construction' with first criticality NOT achieved and no grid connection. World Nuclear News, 3 August 2026, describes it as 'currently undergoing pre-commissioning tests'. Milestones achieved: cold functional testing completed October 2025; world-first non-nuclear turbine steam start-up test completed 23 December 2025. Fuel loading has not been publicly confirmed. Sister large units at the same Changjiang site (unit 3 Hualong One) have overtaken it — Changjiang 3 grid-connected 1 August 2026.
reactors.codnote: CNNC targeted commercial operation in the first half of 2026 (already missed) and China has publicly reconfirmed 2026; the original target was May 2025, so the project is running roughly 1.5 years late. CSIS notes officials acknowledged 'numerous novel challenges' during commissioning. For screening, treat 2026 as at-risk and 2027 as the prudent planning date.

orders.c: CNNC / Hainan Nuclear Power Co. (FOAK demonstration)
orders.n: The only unit built or ordered. Self-funded state demonstration project at Changjiang, Hainan.

No follow-on domestic order has been announced and no export contract is signed. CSIS (May 2026) assesses that 'the lack of continued manufacturing after the first Linglong One deployment makes near-term global exports unlikely'.

reactors.health: Very strong balance sheet and supply chain — CNNC is a central state-owned enterprise with the largest reactor construction programme in the world and complete vertical integration. The commercial risk is not vendor solvency but product commitment: no serial ACP100 production line has been established and no repeat order announced, so supply-chain continuity for a second customer is unproven.
reactors.risks: Schedule slippage of ~1.5 years on a first-of-a-kind that was meant to prove the SMR value proposition; per-MW capital cost is reported to be materially higher than the large Hualong One units next door on the same site, undermining the economic case. steam_temp_c is left null because the once-through SG outlet temperature is not stated in ARIS or the sources checked (secondary pressure 4.6 MPa is verified; a superheated value near 290 C is plausible but was not verified in this pass) — max_process_heat_c of 290 is likewise derived, not a vendor figure. load_following is asserted from CNNC design literature and not independently verified. epz_km is unverified. No follow-on order means an export buyer would be a de facto second FOAK. Absence of Western regulatory precedent makes licensability outside China effectively nil. AUDIT: heaviest-module mass is not disclosed by CNNC or the IAEA; the stored figure is an estimate.
reactors.exp: China is an NSG member (since 2004) and can legally export, but availability is politically bounded. The United States, EU, UK, Japan, Korea, Australia and Canada are closed markets in practice: CNNC is designated on US restricted lists (Chinese military companies / Commerce Entity List exposure), the 2018 US civil-nuclear policy framework curtails nuclear cooperation with CNNC, and no Western regulator has assessed ACP100. Realistic export markets are Belt-and-Road / Global South states with Chinese financing (Pakistan is the established precedent for CNNC exports; Saudi, ASEAN and African interest has been reported but nothing is contracted). Any export creates full dependence on Chinese fuel and services. Practical near-term export probability is low per CSIS.

reactors.ramp_n: No rate published by CNNC or by any regulator I could reach. The IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 ACP100 entry contains no load-following rate, and the NucNet SMR database ACP100 record carries no operational-flexibility figures. Chinese-language academic papers on ACP100 control exist but are not vendor or regulator statements, so I am not converting them into a vendor attribute.
reactors.auto_n: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024, ACP100 entry (CNNC-supplied text): 'The PDHRS provides core cooling for seven (7) days without operator intervention or long term with IRWST' make-up; the in-containment water 'can cope for seven (7) days of cooling in the case of accident before boiling dry and uncovering fuel'; and 'ACP100 has a safety related direct current (DC) power source to support accident mitigation for up to 72 hours, along with auxiliary power units to recharge the battery system for up to seven (7) days.' So 7 days (168 h) with no operator action and 7 days of electrical autonomy - this meets both EUR KP5 targets as claimed. Vendor-stated; China's NNSA has licensed and is commissioning the Hainan Changjiang unit but I found no NNSA document confirming these specific durations.
reactors.avail_n: No availability or capacity factor figure published by CNNC or found in the IAEA entry or the NucNet database record.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Note CGN's EU-HPR1000 (a different vendor and a large reactor) completed an EUR Rev E assessment - not transferable to ACP100.

reactors.name: AP300
reactors.coolant: Light water (scaled single-loop AP1000 architecture, passive safety)
reactors.fuel: UO2 in Westinghouse 17x17 robust fuel assemblies (RFA-2 lineage), same fuel platform as AP1000
reactors.fnote: IAEA ARIS lists 'less than 5 wt.% U-235 in U'. Uses the standard Westinghouse 17x17 PWR fuel platform manufactured today at Columbia SC and Vasteras, with Springfields UK available. No new fuel qualification pathway required. Effectively zero fuel supply risk.
reactors.tnote: Westinghouse markets factory-fabricated modules sized for rail and barge delivery, scaled down from AP1000 modularisation practice (vendor claim). No published heaviest-module mass or dimensional envelope; treat transport class as unverified.

lic.s: Pre-application only. Engagement since May 2023; twelve white papers submitted and NRC feedback complete (including Emergency Planning Zone Definition, core design and fuel cycle, PRA, safety classification). No design certification or design approval application has been docketed, and no target submission date is published. The planned 'Licensing Application Approach' white paper is listed as no longer planned.

Approved to enter GDA and initiated the process in Feb 2024, but the AP300 does not appear among ONR's active, completed or suspended GDA assessments as of Aug 2026 - GDA appears to have not progressed. The AP1000 holds a UK DAC/SoDA from Mar 2017, which Westinghouse leverages commercially.

reactors.cnote: No site anywhere has been selected, permitted or prepared for an AP300. No first concrete, no long-lead procurement announced.
reactors.codnote: No credible date. Westinghouse has never published a firm AP300 COD; its Aug 2026 corporate update quantified a pipeline of up to 91 AP1000-class reactors with CODs from the early 2030s to early 2040s but disclosed no AP300 licensing timeline or first customer. Earlier vendor material pointed at design completion around 2027 and first unit early 2030s (vendor claim).

orders.n: Feb 2024 collaboration to deploy a fleet at a North Teesside site; privately financed, no FID, no construction, no active GDA behind it.
MoU/agreement to pursue AP300 deployment; wartime context, no FID.
Agreement to evaluate AP300 for data-centre deployment; feasibility only.
Feb 2026 MoU to explore AP1000 and AP300 projects in Ontario.

reactors.health: Corporate parent is very strong; the AP300 programme is the weak point. Westinghouse is owned by Brookfield (majority) and Cameco, is the counterparty to an ~USD 80 billion US Government partnership announced Oct 2025 to build an AP1000 fleet, and confidentially filed a draft registration statement with the SEC for an IPO (reported around a USD 30 billion valuation) as announced 5 Aug 2026. It signed collaboration agreements with Amentum in Aug 2026 covering AP1000 fleet delivery and continued AP300 development, with the stated intent to accelerate AP300 NRC licensing. No distress. The real risk is internal prioritisation: essentially all of Westinghouse's announced pipeline, capital and government backing is AP1000, and the AP300 has visibly slipped behind.
reactors.risks: Least advanced of the five on every objective measure: no docketed licensing application in any jurisdiction, no site, no order with an FID, no published COD. UK GDA was entered in Feb 2024 but the design is absent from ONR's current assessment list, which is a material negative signal. Programme is being crowded out by the AP1000 fleet, which now carries an ~USD 80bn government-backed pipeline of up to 91 units and all of Westinghouse's engineering capacity - AP300 progress is dependent on the Amentum partnership adding capacity rather than on Westinghouse's own resourcing. Very long 36-48 month refuelling cycle implies high enrichment/loading demands and reduces flexibility. Footprint, EPZ, air-cooling and module transport figures are all vendor-marketed and unverified. Offsetting strength: the technology risk is the lowest of the set because it is a scaled AP1000 with identical passive safety architecture, licensed fuel and a proven supply chain - if Westinghouse chooses to fund it, it can move faster than its current position suggests.

reactors.ramp_n: No number published. The AP300 brochure and Westinghouse product pages say only 'fast load change capabilities to support variations in demand'. The IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 AP-300 entry notes boron-free-manoeuvre capability ('allows to perform load following manoeuvres without changes to the soluble boron concentration during the manoeuvre, which extends load following capabilities') but gives no rate. The AP1000's published +/-5%/min is a different, larger design and I have deliberately not transferred it.
reactors.minload_n: Not published for AP300 by Westinghouse or any regulator.
reactors.auto_n: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024, AP-300 entry (vendor-supplied text): 'The safety systems are designed to operate for at least 72 hours without AC power' and 'The goal is to ensure the plant safe state to be reached without the need for operator action for all the design basis events.' I record 72 h. The AP1000's familiar '72 h passive / 7 days with on-site resources' split is NOT restated for AP300 in any source I found, so coping_d is left null rather than inherited. UK ONR GDA Step 1 for AP300 was completed but no ONR-confirmed grace/coping figure was located.
reactors.avail_n: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024, AP-300 entry, vendor-supplied bullet: 'Availability, minus planned outages, is expected to be in excess of 97%'. I verified this line sits in the AP-300 section of the catalogue text and not in any other design's entry. Vendor-stated, not regulator-confirmed.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments. Note the parent AP1000 DID complete an EUR Rev C assessment - that is a different design and must not be scored here. AP300's UK ONR GDA entry is a regulatory process, not an EUR assessment.

reactors.name: ARC-100
reactors.fuel: U-10Zr sodium-bonded binary metallic fuel, EBR-II derived; discharge burnup ~77 GWd/tHM
reactors.fnote: Average 13.1 wt% U-235, maximum below 20 wt% (vendor claim). No secured HALEU supply contract and no qualified metallic fuel fabrication route in Canada - CNL is backing fuel development work and a U-10Zr introduction programme, but this is R&D stage. A New Brunswick assessment specifically cited HALEU dependence as a project blocker. Weakest fuel position of the six designs given no build in progress to pull supply forward.
reactors.tnote: Reactor vessel 15.6 m high x 7.6 m diameter - a heavy-lift/barge item. Factory-built modules assembled at a fabrication facility and delivered to site; 34-month construction schedule, 23 months first concrete to fuel load (vendor claim). Module weights not published.

lic.s: Vendor Design Review Phase 2 completed 9 July 2025 (Phase 1 completed Oct 2019, review started Sept 2017). CNSC found 'no fundamental barriers to licensing'. VDR is pre-licensing and confers no authorisation.

Licence to Prepare Site application submitted by NB Power 30 June 2023, still 'awaiting additional submissions from NB Power' as of the CNSC page last modified 26 Jan 2026. Provincial EIA in parallel. Effectively stalled.
Stated intent to license under the 10 CFR Part 53 framework following the final rule in April 2026; no application filed.

reactors.cnote: No construction anywhere. The Point Lepreau demonstration unit, once slated for commissioning by 2029, has effectively lapsed: NB Energy Minister Rene Legacy said in April 2025 the 2030 timeframe 'is probably not going to happen', indicated in October 2025 the province would stop waiting on ARC and Moltex, and a March 2026 NB Power review panel led by former Bruce Power CEO Duncan Hawthorne recommended against SMRs entirely ('We don't think it's appropriate for NB Power to be playing in a first-of-a-kind world'), mentioning SMRs only once in 50 recommendations and steering the province toward proven large-scale nuclear. Roughly C$130M of provincial and federal money has been spent on ARC and Moltex since 2018.
reactors.codnote: The former 2029 Point Lepreau commissioning target is no longer credible. ARC has pivoted toward a US Strategic Partnership Projects contract for a first American deployment, an Alberta industrial partnership with Nucleon Energy, KHNP collaboration and a Turkish term sheet with IC Nuclear & Industry - none of which have a published COD.

orders.n: Partnership since 2018; site licence application filed 2023 but dormant. Provincial government and the March 2026 NB Power review panel have effectively walked away from SMRs. Treat as lapsed, not an order.

orders.c: Nucleon Energy (Alberta industrial), KHNP, IC Nuclear & Industry (Turkey), unnamed US SPP host
orders.n: MOUs, term sheets and a strategic partnership contract only. No FID, no firm unit commitments.

reactors.health: Weak. Small private company (Saint John NB, HQ moved to Washington DC) that has been unable to secure the financial partner needed to carry the Point Lepreau demonstration, per New Brunswick reporting. Loss of its anchor utility customer removes the primary deployment route; the US/Alberta/Korea/Turkey pivot is early-stage. Highest counterparty risk of the six alongside newcleo.
reactors.risks: Anchor customer effectively lost - New Brunswick has publicly turned away from SMRs, leaving no committed host site. No financing partner identified. HALEU supply unsecured and metallic fuel fabrication for Canada is at R&D stage. VDR Phase 2 is pre-licensing only; no licence application by the vendor in any jurisdiction. Twenty-year refuelling interval and in-vessel spent fuel storage are attractive but unproven at commercial scale, and long-life core claims rest on EBR-II heritage rather than modern qualification data.

reactors.name: Aurora Powerhouse (Aurora-INL)
reactors.fuel: Metallic HALEU (U-Zr alloy) pins; first cores from recovered/downblended EBR-II fuel, fabricated at Oklo's Aurora Fuel Fabrication Facility at INL
reactors.fnote: Three-track strategy: (1) DOE-allocated recovered EBR-II HALEU for first cores, (2) commercial HALEU - letter of intent with Centrus for American Centrifuge Plant material 'enough to support up to five Aurora powerhouses for multiple years' with potential 2029 deliveries (vendor claim), (3) recycling - Oklo was selected by DOE for negotiations on ~20 tonnes of surplus plutonium as bridge fuel, and has an Aurora Fuel Fabrication Facility (NSDA approved Nov 2025) plus a private recycling facility announced. Metallic fuel fabrication capacity is captive and not yet built at scale; Centrus deliveries are an LOI, not a contract. mwth_module is an estimate derived from 75 MWe at ~40% cycle efficiency - Oklo has not published a thermal rating.
reactors.tnote: Reactor module and Siemens SST-600 turbine island are heavy-lift/rail items; Oklo states ~70% of powerhouse components come from non-nuclear industrial supply chains. Module weights not published.

lic.s: Aurora-INL is being authorized by DOE, not NRC: Other Transaction Agreement signed, Nuclear Safety Design Agreement approved, Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis approved June 2026, DOE approval for final design and construction received.

Pre-application only. The original 2020 Aurora COLA was DENIED without prejudice on 6 Jan 2022. NRC readiness assessment completed July 2025; Principal Design Criteria topical report approved 2026; as of April 2026 no new COLA had been submitted. Aurora-Ohio (1.2 GWe campus) is preparing for NRC pre-application review.

reactors.cnote: Groundbreaking at Idaho National Laboratory on 22 September 2025; as of mid-2026 in deep-foundation excavation with Kiewit as construction partner. Siemens Energy SST-600 turbine / SGen-100A generator package under binding contract. Note that Oklo's August 2026 'first criticality' milestone was at the Groves isotope facility in Texas (5 Aug 2026, Atomic Alchemy subsidiary), NOT Aurora - Aurora remains pre-criticality. 2026 capex guidance raised to $400-500M.
reactors.codnote: Oklo targets Aurora-INL commercial operations in 2028 (vendor claim). Management declined to give updated total project cost guidance at Q2 2026, and DOE-pathway authorization does not confer an NRC licence for follow-on commercial sites.

orders.n: Master power agreement for up to 12 GW of Aurora capacity through 2044 - a framework, not firm orders or FID; unit count not fixed.

orders.c: Data-centre and defence customers (Equinix, Diamondback Energy, Eielson AFB / USAF, Liberty and others)
orders.n: Multi-GW non-binding pipeline; CFO described demand as 'in a sense unconstrained'. No customer has taken FID on a specific unit beyond Aurora-INL, which Oklo is building for its own account.

reactors.health: Very strong liquidity, no revenue. NYSE-listed (OKLO). At 30 June 2026: $3.0bn cash and securities, $3.4bn total assets, $3.3bn stockholders' equity, current ratio ~60; ~$1.9bn raised via ATM programs in 2026. H1 2026 net loss $81.6M on $124.2M operating loss. Operating cash burn guidance raised to $120-150M. First revenue (isotopes, not power) expected early 2027. Equity-funded build-own-operate model means dilution risk if capital markets tighten.
reactors.risks: No NRC licence - the 2022 COLA denial has not been cured and commercial fleet deployment outside DOE sites depends on an as-yet-unsubmitted COLA; DOE-pathway precedent may not transfer. Fuel: first cores depend on DOE-supplied recovered EBR-II material and a captive fabrication plant not yet operating; Centrus supply is an LOI. FOAK cost undisclosed. Build-own-operate model means Oklo carries full construction and merchant risk on its own balance sheet. Aurora has never gone critical; Groves criticality is a much smaller, different machine. Very large non-binding backlog versus one unit actually under construction.

reactors.name: BANR (BWXT Advanced Nuclear Reactor) and Project Pele transportable microreactor
reactors.vendor: BWX Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: BWXT) / BWXT Advanced Technologies LLC
reactors.fuel: Uranium nitride (UN) TRISO particles in a densified matrix, produced with advanced additive and chemical processes (BANR); TRISO compacts for Project Pele — BWXT delivered ~40,000 TRISO fuel compacts for the Pele core
reactors.fnote: Strongest fuel position of the US designs here: BWXT operates the established TRISO manufacturing line at Lynchburg, Virginia, has commissioned new furnace capacity with DOE support, delivered a FULL core of TRISO fuel for Project Pele (announced 2 Dec 2025; 40,000 compacts shipped to INL 5 Nov 2025), and manufactured the TRISO fuel that enabled the first new reactor criticality under the DOE pilot programme (Antares Mark-0, June 2026). Caveat: BANR's specific UN TRISO in a densified matrix is a different and less mature fuel than the UCO/UO2 TRISO already produced — BWXT's Fuel Qualification Topical Report for BANR was planned for 4Q 2028, so BANR fuel qualification, not fabrication capacity, is the gating item. HALEU feedstock for commercial BANR volumes is not secured publicly.
reactors.tnote: BANR: factory-assembled skid-based design that 'transports within five modules, each meeting road and rail shipping requirements' (vendor claim) — this road/rail constraint is the design driver behind the 50 MWth rating. Project Pele is more aggressively transportable: it fits in four standard 20-foot ISO shipping containers and is designed for truck, rail and airlift, meeting military shock and vibration requirements.

lic.s: Pre-application engagement only for BANR — NRC licensing kick-off meeting held 2022, fuel qualification white paper 4Q2023, Fuel Qualification Topical Report planned 4Q2028. NO construction permit application had been filed as of Aug 2026.
Project Pele is authorised under DOE/DoD authority at Idaho National Laboratory rather than NRC-licensed; environmental review completed and site groundbreaking held at INL

reactors.cnote: IMPORTANT — this status applies to Project Pele, NOT to BANR. Pele: core manufacturing started Aug 2025 at BWXT Lynchburg, VA; core stacking completed June 2026; full TRISO core delivered to INL 5 Nov 2025 (announced 2 Dec 2025); reactor to ship from Lynchburg to INL for testing. On schedule against the 30 Sept 2028 delivery deadline set by Executive Order 14299. BANR itself has no site, no permit and no construction — it remains in design/development under DOE ARDP (risk-reduction award).
reactors.codnote: Project Pele: formal system testing targeted for early 2027 with electricity production as soon as 2028; delivery deadline 30 Sept 2028. BANR commercial deployment is indicated for the 'early 2030s' via the Tata Chemicals Wyoming discussions, with no committed date. NOTE: mwe_module = 17 is an ESTIMATE — BWXT publishes 50 MWth per BANR reactor and does not publish an electrical rating; 17 MWe assumes ~34% net efficiency. Project Pele is separately rated at 1.5 MWe minimum.

orders.c: US Department of Defense / Department of War, Strategic Capabilities Office (Project Pele)
orders.n: Fully funded government prototype, hardware built and fuel delivered. Executed contract, not a commercial order.

orders.c: Tata Chemicals Soda Ash Partners LLC (Green River, Wyoming soda ash plant)
orders.n: Letter of intent signed 17 Dec 2024 to develop commercial terms for conditional purchase of up to eight 50 MWt BANR units for power and process heat; deployment indicated for the early 2030s. Exploratory — no FID, no energy purchase agreement yet.

orders.c: Wyoming Energy Authority / State of Wyoming
orders.n: Contract awarded 2023 to evaluate microreactor deployment in Wyoming; Burns & McDonnell engaged to advance BANR development. Study-stage.

reactors.health: By far the strongest and most conventional of the five: BWXT is a profitable, publicly traded NYSE company and a long-standing sole-source supplier of naval nuclear reactors and fuel to the US Navy, with existing licensed nuclear manufacturing plants in Lynchburg VA and Canada. It carries no startup financing risk and is frequently characterised as the incumbent 'veteran' in the advanced reactor field. Its advanced-reactor programmes are a small part of a large defence-anchored business, which cuts both ways — durable, but BANR competes internally for capital and is not existential to the company.
reactors.risks: BANR and Pele must not be conflated. Pele is real hardware nearing test but is a 1.5 MWe military prototype with no commercial licensing pathway; BANR is a commercial 50 MWth product that has filed NO NRC construction permit application and whose fuel qualification topical report was scheduled only for 4Q2028 — a very long runway to a commercial deployment. BANR's electrical rating, core outlet temperature, module weights, footprint and EPZ are all unpublished; the 750 °C outlet and 17 MWe figures used here are inferred from the HTGR class and should be flagged as unverified. UN TRISO in a densified matrix is a novel fuel form requiring qualification. The only commercial demand signal is a non-binding LOI from Tata Chemicals. Air-cooling assumed true from the remote/industrial deployment framing, not from an explicit source. AUDIT: construction status refers to the Project Pele prototype, not to commercial BANR, which has no licence application.

reactors.name: BWRX-300
reactors.fuel: GNF2 UO2 BWR fuel bundles, 240 bundles, 3.8 m active height
reactors.fnote: GNF2 is a commercially produced, already-licensed BWR fuel in worldwide service; Global Nuclear Fuel lines in Wilmington NC and Kurihama JP. IAEA ARIS lists 3.8% average / 4.95% maximum enrichment. Lowest fuel-supply risk of any SMR in this set.
reactors.tnote: RPV is ~4.2 m ID x ~27.4 m tall - too large for road/rail as a single piece; forged rings (Doosan Enerbility, IHI) are shipped by sea/barge and field-welded. Darlington and Clinch River are both waterfront sites. GVH claims most other modules are rail/truck shippable (vendor claim). Heaviest single lift not publicly disclosed.

lic.s: Licence to Construct issued for Darlington Unit 1; Regulatory Hold Point-1 cleared Mar 2026; Licence to Operate application submitted Mar 2026
TVA Clinch River construction permit: application docketed Jul 2025, Final SEIS Apr 2026, Final Safety Evaluation Report 25 Jun 2026, mandatory hearing 13 Aug 2026, permit decision targeted Fall 2026
GDA statement issued (2-step GDA completed)

reactors.cnote: Darlington Unit 1 (Ontario, Canada) is the only SMR of this set physically under nuclear construction. Excavation of all three major shafts completed Mar 2026; the 2.1 million lb diaphragm-plate steel-composite basemat was placed Apr 2026. Units 2-4 not yet started. Nth-of-a-kind construction claim of 24-36 months from first nuclear concrete to fuel load is unproven (vendor claim).
reactors.codnote: OPG targets construction complete by end of 2029 and grid connection by end of 2030 for Darlington Unit 1. Clinch River COD not firm pending Fall 2026 permit decision. Poland (OSGE) has publicly cited 2029-2030 for a Wloclawek pilot, widely regarded as optimistic (vendor/developer claim).

orders.n: FID/funding approval May 2025; CAD 6.1bn for Unit 1 plus CAD 1.6bn common facilities; CAD 20.9bn for all four. Unit 1 under construction.
Construction permit recommended by NRC staff Jun 2026; TVA has not taken a full FID on plant completion.
Polish generic design agreement signed Mar 2026; ~24 units across six sites aspirational, no FID.
BWRX-300 selected as technology; target ~2035, no FID.
Technology selected; provincial construction decision not before ~2029.
Shortlisted alongside Rolls-Royce SMR; no award.
MoU / feasibility only.

reactors.health: Strongest of the set. GE Vernova (NYSE: GEV) is a large-cap, profitable, investment-grade listed company that raised full-year 2026 financial guidance with its Q2 2026 results on 22 Jul 2026; nuclear sits inside its Power segment and is not dependent on external SMR-specific funding. GVH is a JV with Hitachi. No distress, bankruptcy or layoff signals in the nuclear business; principal corporate risk is portfolio prioritisation rather than solvency.
reactors.risks: Natural-circulation BWR stability at startup and low power was flagged by the NRC ACRS as needing resolution at the operating-licence stage and initial startup - a genuine first-of-a-kind technical open item. Load following is slow (0.5%/min between 50-90% power, 2%/min above 90%), so it is a poor fit for fast-ramping duty. Direct-cycle BWR means turbine-hall and any process-steam loop are radiologically active, which limits industrial steam export to indirect (secondary) heat exchange. EPZ size is not settled - Canada uses a detailed planning zone and the US site-boundary EPZ case has not been adjudicated; treat epz_km as unknown. Air-cooling capability is vendor-stated, not independently confirmed. RPV cannot be factory-shipped whole, so waterfront or very heavy-lift access is effectively required. Darlington Unit 1 cost of CAD 6.1bn for 300 MWe (~USD 15,000/kW FOAK) is a serious economic risk marker. AUDIT: air/dry-cooling capability is not confirmed by GE Vernova Hitachi or a regulator; both lead sites are water-cooled.

reactors.ramp_n: GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 General Description: 'the speed limitations of the FMCRDs limit power maneuvers to (at most) 0.5% power/minute for load following between 50-90% power or 2% power/minute for load changes between 90-100% power.' The sustained load-following rate over the wide band is therefore 0.5 %Pr/min; 2 %Pr/min applies only in the narrow 90-100% band. No unit conversion needed - vendor states %/min directly. Neither figure meets EUR KP14's 3 %Pr/min over a wide band.
reactors.minload_n: Derived, not directly stated. GEH does not publish a minimum stable power level. The lowest bound of the vendor's stated load-following band is 50% power, so 50 %Pr is the lowest power for which a manoeuvring rate is given. Reactor power reduction (control rods), not steam bypass.
reactors.auto_n: BWRX-300 General Description: 'With two ICS trains in service, decay heat removal is sustained for seven days without operator action.' IAEA ARIS SMR Catalogue 2024 BWRX-300 entry: Isolation Condenser System provides cooling 'for at least seven days for all design basis accidents'; 'Emergency Power System ensures 72-hour battery-backed DC and UPS AC power'. 7 days = 168 h is a vendor-stated analysed value, not a marketing 'unlimited' claim.
reactors.avail_n: No vendor or regulator availability/capacity-factor figure found. reactors.name: CMSR Power Barge (Compact Molten Salt Reactor)
reactors.coolant: Liquid fluoride fuel salt (uranium fluoride in Li-7 fluoride carrier) circulating through a moderator salt/graphite core; FLiNaK secondary coolant salt; steam generator to high-pressure water. Ultimate heat sink is seawater.
reactors.fuel: Liquid fluoride fuel salt, LEU as uranium fluoride dissolved in Li-7 fluoride carrier; design switched from HALEU to LEU in early 2023 explicitly because of HALEU supply risk
reactors.fnote: Uranium side is the easy part: Seaborg/Saltfoss deliberately abandoned HALEU in early 2023 and moved to standard LEU (<5%) precisely because HALEU availability was judged too risky - a sound call. The binding constraint is Li-7. World Nuclear Association describes the CMSR fuel salt as 'Li-7 fluoride initially with uranium as fluoride', so the design sits squarely on the enriched-lithium bottleneck: Russia's TVEL Novosibirsk Chemical Concentrates Plant supplies up to 80% of world Li-7 hydroxide (99.95% purity) and China is the only other producer (and reportedly buys substantially from Russia). Neither source is realistically available to a Danish/Korean commercial project. Global Li-7 demand today is ~1 tonne/year for PWR chemistry control; a commercialised MSR fleet implies tens of tonnes per reactor and up to ~250 t/yr, with MSR fluoride purity requirements up to 99.995%. The historic COLEX mercury-amalgam route is banned in the US; Western alternatives (AVLIS - e.g. Hexium, which raised USD 12M; crown-ether extraction; centrifugal extraction) are pre-commercial with 3-5 year self-declared timelines. Secondary FLiNaK coolant also contains lithium, compounding the requirement. Additional unproven element: the molten NaOH moderator concept (now reportedly revised toward graphite) has no operating precedent and carries unresolved corrosion questions.
reactors.tnote: The plant is the transport: shipping-container-scale reactor modules integrated into a purpose-built barge hull by a shipyard (Samsung Heavy Industries), then towed to the customer's coastline and moored. 2-8 reactors of 100 MWe per hull, up to ~800 MWe per platform. Eliminates site civil works but introduces flag-state/IMO and host-state dual-regulation problems that have no precedent outside Russia's Akademik Lomonosov.

lic.s: Declared 'ready to start licensing activities with the nuclear authorities in South Korea'; no formal Standard Design Approval application confirmed as accepted, no docket identified
None - Denmark has no nuclear power licensing regime in force for commercial reactors

reactors.cnote: No nuclear construction and no shipyard steel cut. Conceptual design reported complete as of late 2025; company is in design maturation and licensing preparation.
reactors.codnote: Guidance has slipped repeatedly: 2020 guidance said 2025; 2023 guidance said 2028 commercial operation; by 2025 the CEO conceded 2028 was 'a commercial wish' and now targets first reactor in the first half of the 2030s with series production from the mid-2030s (vendor claim). 2032 is the vendor's optimistic end of that range; 2035+ is the defensible planning assumption.

orders.c: Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power / Samsung Heavy Industries
orders.n: Consortium agreement to develop CMSR-based floating nuclear power plants - manufacturing and operating partnership, not a purchase order. No FID.
Feasibility study only, targeting completion by 2035. No units committed, no FID.

reactors.health: Fragile but NOT insolvent as of August 2026 - the notable corporate event is a rebrand, not a bankruptcy. Seaborg Technologies renamed itself Saltfoss Energy on 3 April 2025. Around the same time the founding leadership turned over: founder and former CEO Troels Schonfeldt left the board in February 2025, Niels de Conninck-Smith became chairman (February 2025) and former Aarhus mayor Jacob Bundesgaard joined the board. The company raised approximately DKK 200M (USD ~29.7M) from existing investors in February 2025 - an insider round, not a priced new-investor round, which is a negative signal on external appetite. Cumulative support and investment since founding is reported at over DKK 500M. Headcount roughly 60-75 across Copenhagen and Geoje-si, South Korea. A detailed October 2025 Danish investigative piece (videnskab.dk) documented the repeated timeline slippage and the retreat from the original thorium/waste-burning claims to conventional LEU, and reported that when asked what the remaining obstacle was, the team answered in unison: 'Money'. No administration, receivership, konkurs or rekonstruktion filing was found in searches of Danish and English sources through August 2026. Assessment: capital-constrained, leadership-churned and schedule-slipped, but a going concern.
reactors.risks: Financing is the acknowledged binding constraint - last round was an insider round of ~USD 30M against a first-of-a-kind floating reactor programme that needs orders of magnitude more. Li-7 fuel-salt and FLiNaK coolant supply is hostage to Russian/Chinese producers. The NaOH-moderator concept that differentiated the design has been walked back toward graphite, eroding the original claim. Founder and CEO departure plus board reconstitution in early 2025 signals a strategy reset. No accepted regulatory docket anywhere - the Korean pathway is stated intent only. Floating/marine nuclear licensing across flag state, coastal state and IMO has essentially no commercial precedent. Timeline has slipped ~7 years in five years of guidance.

reactors.name: Copenhagen Atomics Onion Core (containerised thorium MSR)
reactors.fuel: Liquid thorium fluoride fuel salt; 5% enriched uranium (LEU) driver fuel salt with thorium blanket salt, thermal spectrum, burn-then-breed toward U-233; optional transuranic feed from spent fuel
reactors.fnote: The most Li-7-exposed design in this set and the least mature fuel supply position alongside Moltex. The base salt is explicitly 'F7LiTh' - ThF4 plus isotopically enriched 7LiF - and the company's own public materials state that '99.999% Lithium 7' is an essential step toward its USD 20/MWh cost target. That is a purity above the ~99.95% grade that Russia's TVEL Novosibirsk Chemical Concentrates Plant supplies for PWR chemistry and above the 99.95% used in China's TMSR-LF1. Only Russia and China produce enriched Li-7 at all, Russia covers up to 80% of world supply, and that material is not available for Western nuclear development; China's SINAP has demonstrated centrifugal extraction to 99.99%. The US banned the mercury-amalgam COLEX route decades ago; Western replacements - AVLIS (Hexium, USD 12M raised, self-declared 3-5 years to materially reduce foreign reliance), crown-ether extraction (regarded as the better route for large MSR fluoride volumes), and Precision Periodic's DOE-backed process - are all pre-commercial. Against a global Li-7 market of roughly 1 tonne per year today and tens of tonnes required per MSR, a fleet of 100 MWth Copenhagen Atomics units implies a Li-7 industry that does not exist in the West and would have to be built essentially from zero. Compounding this: the design is a thorium breeder requiring U-233 handling, online salt chemistry processing and a fuel-cycle back end for which no commercial vendor exists anywhere. Uranium driver fuel at 5% is the only uncontroversial element.
reactors.tnote: Core commercial premise is containerised mass manufacture - the reactor is designed to ship in standard 40-foot shipping containers with no onsite assembly, only installation; the company describes a 100 MWth unit envelope of about 30 x 7 x 7 m including a 12-section radiation shield, and a build time of 6-18 months per reactor (vendor claim). No published transport weights. Aspiration of 'one reactor per day' mass production is a marketing position, not an engineering plan.

lic.s: SMR design submitted to the UK Generic Design Assessment process; entry to GDA not confirmed as granted

Four-year collaboration agreement with PSI to run the first critical thorium molten salt reactor experiment in Europe using the Onion Core design; experiments originally scheduled 2026-27, company website now indicates a 1 MWth test reactor at PSI in 2028. Research experiment, not a power reactor licence.

reactors.cnote: No nuclear construction and no critical experiment yet performed. Progress is in non-fission full-scale prototypes and component endurance testing: a third prototype is under construction, the company reports over 160,000 cumulative component test-days, announced two years of continuous molten salt pump operation on 9 February 2026, and announced corrosion mitigation via salt-purity optimisation on 4 March 2026. Credible, disciplined component engineering - but the reactor has never gone critical.
reactors.codnote: Company targets a 1 MWth test reactor at PSI in 2028 and commercial 100 MWth units in the early 2030s (vendor claim). Historic guidance has slipped substantially - 2022 public slides showed a 1 MW test reactor in 2025, first commercial reactor in 2027, mass manufacturing in 2030 and a USD 20/MWh breeder by 2033-2036. Applying the observed slip rate, commercial operation before the late 2030s is not supportable.

orders.n: Research collaboration for a 1 MWth critical experiment, not a commercial order. No FID.
Older company slides referenced '25 customers' with no names, volumes or contract status disclosed - treat as marketing pipeline, not orders (vendor claim).

reactors.health: Private, small and technically credible but under-capitalised for the ambition. Roughly 75 engineers, over 200 investors across 20 countries, EUR 20M Series A in January 2023, and a European Innovation Council Accelerator award announced 2 July 2025. Recognised with a Reuters Global Energy Award in June 2025. No disclosed large institutional round and no revenue. Funding scale is an order of magnitude or more below what a licensed critical experiment plus commercial FOAK requires.
reactors.risks: Li-7 at 99.999% purity is a hard dependency on an industry that does not exist outside Russia and China - this alone can gate the programme regardless of engineering progress. No critical experiment has been performed, so all neutronics and fuel-cycle claims are unvalidated; the PSI experiment has already slipped from 2026-27 to 2028. Thorium/U-233 breeding with online salt processing is the most technically ambitious fuel cycle of the six and has no commercial precedent. Heavy-water moderator combined with molten fluoride salt is an unusual combination with limited materials data. UK GDA submission has not been confirmed as accepted into the process. Funding is far below programme needs and the timeline has slipped roughly five years in four years of guidance. The USD 20/MWh LCOE claim is not credible on current evidence.

reactors.name: eVinci Microreactor
reactors.fuel: UCO TRISO particles in compacts within a monolithic hexagonal graphite core block
reactors.fnote: 19.75% HALEU TRISO. TRISO fabrication is the most mature advanced-fuel route in North America (BWXT and X-energy TF3 lines) which is a relative advantage, but the HALEU feedstock is the same constrained pool as every other design: Centrus reached its 900 kg Phase 2 DOE milestone in January 2026 and received a $900M DOE award (alongside Orano Federal Services and General Matter at $900M each), while Urenco's New Mexico expansion is not expected fully operational until ~2030. An 8-year whole-core cartridge means large discrete fuel loads per unit rather than a steady annual draw. Westinghouse has manufactured the first ever 12-foot nuclear-grade heat pipe (vendor claim).
reactors.tnote: Fully factory-assembled and transportable in standard shipping containers by rail, barge and truck, with fuel installed; above-ground installation with less than a 2-3 acre footprint and under 12 months from first concrete to criticality (vendor claim). Individual module masses not published.

lic.s: Advanced Logic System (ALS) Version 2 I&C platform approved December 2024 - first and only microreactor with an NRC-approved I&C system. Principal Design Criteria topical report approved April 2025. No construction permit or COL application filed for a commercial unit.

Preliminary Safety Design Report approved by DOE 5 June 2025 - first microreactor developer to achieve this for the NRIC-DOME test bed at INL. Draft Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis in preparation (third of four required DOE submissions). DOME facility expected ready for testing in 2026. Test unit is a scaled 3 MWt article, not the 5 MWe product.
Vendor Design Review engagement; design also listed as under design certification review per IAEA ARIS. Pre-licensing only.

reactors.cnote: No nuclear unit under construction. Nearest-term hardware is the scaled 3 MWt test reactor for the NRIC-DOME facility at Idaho National Laboratory, pending the remaining DOE safety submissions. Westinghouse also operates a microreactor 'accelerator hub' and has partnered with Radiant on early US microreactor testing.
reactors.codnote: IAEA ARIS lists projected commercialisation in 2029 (vendor claim). That depends on successful DOME testing plus an NRC licensing route for a commercial unit that has not yet been opened with an application.

orders.c: US Air Force / Defense Innovation Unit - Malmstrom AFB
orders.n: Selected 23 April 2026 under the Advanced Nuclear Power for Installations (ANPI) programme; next phase of an existing Westinghouse Government Services contract covering siting and construction feasibility assessment. A selection and feasibility phase, not a construction order.
Partnership formalised March 2025 to site an eVinci on campus for research and power; letter of intent submitted to NRC 28 February 2025. No licence application or FID.
First Canadian eVinci targeted for Saskatchewan under agreements dating to 2022. No FID; also an MOU with McMaster University.

reactors.health: Strongest vendor balance sheet in the set. Westinghouse is owned by Brookfield Renewable and Cameco, with a large AP1000 and fuel/services business funding eVinci development - no going-concern or financing risk at the parent level. Risk is prioritisation rather than solvency: eVinci competes internally with the AP1000 fleet programme for capital and engineering resource, and Westinghouse has moved slowly relative to venture-backed microreactor rivals (Antares, Valar Atomics and Deployable Energy all achieved DOE-authorized criticality before the 4 July 2026 Reactor Pilot Program deadline, while eVinci has not).
reactors.risks: No nuclear unit built or licensed - the entire programme still hinges on the scaled 3 MWt DOME test article, and competitors have already reached criticality. No NRC construction permit or COL application for a commercial unit means the commercial licensing path is untested end-to-end. Heat pipe technology at scale is the key first-of-a-kind engineering risk: several thousand sodium heat pipes per core, with failure propagation, freeze-thaw and long-duration creep behaviour unproven over an 8-year core life. Economics at 5 MWe require high-volume factory production and repeat orders that do not yet exist - current 'orders' are feasibility studies, LOIs and MOUs. HALEU TRISO cost and availability at fleet scale is unresolved. Upside: no water needed, sub-3-acre footprint, 20-100% load following at 20%/minute, containerised transport and the highest outlet temperature in this set make it the best process-heat and off-grid fit.

reactors.ramp_n: No rate published. The IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 eVinci entry makes repeated load-following claims - 'capability for load following and grid frequency control', 'can perform load following for the most demanding situations in remote applications', 'Load following logic autonomously adjusts control drum position based on load variances' - but gives no %/min or MW/min figure anywhere. CAUTION: a '10% of reactor nominal power per minute' figure and a '1 MWe/min' figure both appear in the same catalogue, but they belong to the HOLOS-Quad microreactor entry, not to eVinci; I checked the section boundaries and did not transfer them.
reactors.minload_n: Not published. The claimed mechanism is control-drum adjustment by an autonomous control system (reactor power reduction), and Westinghouse notes 'Most of the load following demands can be executed utilizing the self-control' characteristics of the heat-pipe core - but no minimum power level is stated.
reactors.auto_n: No hour or day figure published. The IAEA eVinci entry states the design has 'no safety related operator actions and minimal daily activities to perform'. That is a claim about the absence of credited operator actions, not a quantified grace period, and Westinghouse attaches no duration. eVinci is in NRC pre-application; no regulator-confirmed value found. Not converted.
reactors.avail_n: No availability or capacity factor percentage published for eVinci.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Out of EUR SMLWR scope (heat-pipe-cooled transportable micro reactor - explicitly excluded by the Key Positions).

reactors.name: HTR-PM (Shidaowan / Shidao Bay demonstration plant)
reactors.vendor: Tsinghua University Institute of Nuclear and New Energy Technology
reactors.fuel: 60 mm spherical graphite pebbles, each containing ~12,000 four-layer ceramic-coated (TRISO) particles and ~7 g of heavy metal; over 400,000 pebbles per reactor module
reactors.fnote: The only design here with a fully proven, operating industrial fuel supply chain. CNNC manufactures the pebbles at a dedicated plant (Baotou, Inner Mongolia) and has been supplying the operating plant continuously since 2021. Crucially, HTR-PM uses only 8.5% enriched uranium, so it sidesteps the HALEU bottleneck entirely — an important contrast with all four US designs. Fuel supply is not a constraint on this design; export availability outside China is the constraint.
reactors.tnote: Not a transportable design — large site-erected steel reactor pressure vessels and once-through helical steam generators delivered as heavy components to a coastal site. No published module weights in the sources reviewed. Included as the reference operating HTGR, not as a modular-transport comparator.

lic.s: Licensed and operating — construction start Dec 2012; reactor 1 first criticality 12 Sept 2021, reactor 2 first criticality 11 Nov 2021; grid connection 20 Dec 2021; full power 9 Dec 2022; commercial operation Dec 2023

HTR-PM600 (six modules, ~650 MWe, ~43.7% thermal efficiency) feasibility work at candidate sites including Ruijin (Jiangxi), Wan'an (Fujian), Sanmen (Zhejiang) and Xiapu (Fujian). No confirmed construction start for an HTR-PM600 was found in this research.

reactors.cnote: World's first modular high-temperature gas-cooled reactor plant in commercial operation. Configuration is two 250 MWth reactor modules feeding a single 210 MWe steam turbine (i.e. ~105 MWe per module; the plant has at times been reported operating at 2 × 200 MWth rather than full 2 × 250 MWth). Also demonstrated as a heat source: an associated district-heating project has been commissioned. This is the only entry in this database with real operating experience, and it is the primary empirical evidence base for pebble-bed HTGR behaviour, online refuelling and passive decay-heat removal.
reactors.codnote: Achieved — commercial operation December 2023. Reported design thermal efficiency ~40% for the demonstration plant; HTR-PM600 targets ~43.7%.

orders.c: China Huaneng Group (Shidao Bay, Shandong) — demonstration plant
orders.n: Two reactor modules, one turbine, built and operating. Owner-operator Huaneng; CNNC provided EPC and fuel; Tsinghua INET provided the design.

orders.c: HTR-PM600 candidate sites (Ruijin, Wan'an, Sanmen, Xiapu)
orders.n: Feasibility/site-study stage for six-module ~650 MWe commercial units. INET cost estimate: 15-20% more than a 600 MWe PWR for the first unit, dropping to roughly half of the demonstration plant's ~$6000/kW for later units (developer estimate).

reactors.health: State-backed and structurally secure — Tsinghua INET (design), CNNC (EPC and fuel) and China Huaneng (owner-operator) are all major state entities with no commercial solvency risk. The relevant risk is not corporate but commercial: follow-on HTR-PM600 deployment has been slow relative to earlier announcements, and China's build programme has prioritised Hualong One PWRs (a second Hualong One started construction at the same Shidaowan site in 2025), which suggests the HTGR line is not currently the priority technology domestically.
reactors.risks: For screening purposes the risks are commercial and geopolitical rather than technical. Not exportable to or licensable in the US/EU in any realistic timeframe; no Western regulatory pedigree. Follow-on HTR-PM600 has not reached construction despite ~2.5 years of demonstration-plant operation, which weakens the 'proven scaling path' argument. Steam conditions are excellent but slightly below the Xe-100's claimed 565 °C/165 bar in pressure terms (HTR-PM ~566 °C at ~13.2 MPa); note that sources vary between 565 °C/13.2 MPa and 566 °C/13.25 MPa. Reported operation at 2 × 200 MWth rather than the 2 × 250 MWth design rating deserves verification — sustained derating would be a material data point for pebble-bed HTGR performance. Detailed capacity-factor and availability data for 2024-2026 were not obtainable from open Western sources in this research, which is itself a screening limitation. Seawater-cooled coastal site; air cooling not applicable.

reactors.ramp_n: No vendor or regulator rate found. The IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 HTR-PM entry (INET/Tsinghua) contains no load-following rate. A peer-reviewed load-following control strategy for HTR-PM has been published (Energy, 2022) but that is an academic control study, not an INET or NNSA statement, so I have not converted it into a vendor attribute.
reactors.minload_n: Not published by INET/Tsinghua. The two-module-one-turbine arrangement at Shidaowan means plant output can in principle be halved by taking a module off, but no minimum stable power level is stated.
reactors.auto_n: No hour or day figure published. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 HTR-PM entry lists Distinguishing features as 'Inherent safety, no need for offsite emergency measures' and notes the temperature coefficient is negative with two independent shutdown systems - all qualitative. HTR-PM is in commercial operation and China's NNSA has licensed it, but I found no published NNSA-confirmed grace or coping duration. Not converted.
reactors.avail_n: No percentage published. The IAEA entry says only that with the online refuelling mode of HTR-PM 'better availability factor can be expected compared with other power plants' - a qualitative comparison, not a number.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Out of EUR SMLWR scope (gas-cooled).

reactors.name: i-SMR (Innovative Small Modular Reactor)
reactors.vendor: i-SMR Development Agency, Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power, and Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute
reactors.fuel: UO2 in 17x17 assemblies (260 fuel rod positions); 69 assemblies, 49 control rod assemblies; soluble-boron-free core using burnable absorbers
reactors.fnote: Standard <5% LEU UO2 (typical 4.95 w/o) in conventional 17x17 geometry — supplied by KEPCO NF domestically with Westinghouse/Framatome as alternates. No fuel-qualification risk. Note Korea has no domestic enrichment (US 123 Agreement constraints), so front-end depends on imported EUP.
reactors.tnote: Integral 540 MWt module with in-vessel SGs — a large forging requiring heavy-lift/barge delivery, not truck- or rail-shippable. Vendor claims 24-month construction for the first module and 48 months for a four-module 680 MWe plant, one-third the capex and half the build time of a large reactor (vendor claim). Module weights and dimensions not published in the ARIS datasheet.

lic.s: Standard Design Approval (SDA) application submitted; NSSC document-suitability review before full-scale evaluation. Approval targeted 2028.
Standard design completed end-2025; SMR Act passed to create a dedicated licensing framework
Detailed design with pre-licensing review under way; all engineered safety functions passive, no AC/DC power needed for 72 h; EPZ at site boundary; 80-year design life

reactors.cnote: No concrete. Major de-risking step on 18 June 2026: Korea's site selection committee designated Gijang-gun, Busan as the site for the country's first SMR plant (~700 MWe, i.e. four i-SMR modules), alongside Yeongdeok for two large reactors. Site is selected but no construction permit application has been filed; the SDA must complete first.
reactors.codnote: The Gijang SMR is scheduled under Korea's 11th Basic Plan for Electricity (2024-2038) for completion by 2038. KHNP separately targets mid-2030s commercialisation, and a Daegu MoU (June 2024) envisages a 680 MWe four-module plant with commercial development beginning 2033. Treat 2035 as the earliest credible FOAK and 2038 as the planned date.

orders.n: Site formally selected 18 Jun 2026 for a ~700 MWe SMR plant under the 11th Basic Plan; national-programme commitment but no construction permit or FID yet. This is the anchor project.
MoU June 2024 for a 680 MWe (4-module) facility, commercial development from 2033. Feasibility stage only.
Cooperation agreement Jan 2025 on i-SMR introduction, site pre-feasibility and 'SMR Smart Net-zero City' models. Non-binding.
Cooperation agreement Jan 2025; targets early-2030s first commercial operation. Non-binding. NOTE: EU market is largely blocked for KHNP by the Westinghouse settlement — see export_restrictions.
KHNP has signed i-SMR evaluation agreements; no orders.

reactors.health: Strong. KHNP is state-owned (KEPCO group), operates ~26 reactors, and holds a live large-reactor export backlog (Czech Dukovany 5&6, Barakah track record). The i-SMR programme is a funded national programme with KAERI. Principal commercial overhang is the January 2025 global settlement with Westinghouse (and the associated US DOE understanding), which caps addressable markets and imposes per-reactor licensing/procurement payments.
reactors.risks: Steam-cycle conditions (steam temperature/pressure) are not published in the ARIS datasheet — max_process_heat_c of 285 C here is DERIVED from the 321 C core outlet, not a vendor figure. epz_km is entered as 0 because ARIS states the EPZ is at the site boundary; this is a design target that NSSC has not yet approved and must be re-verified. Other risks: SDA approval not expected before 2028 and NSSC has no prior integral-SMR licensing precedent; soluble-boron-free core physics is novel for KHNP at this scale; the Gijang site faces local-acceptance and grid questions; 170 MWe/module means a fully modular four-pack, so FOAK cost is spread over an unproven multi-module construction sequence; export addressable market is legally restricted.
reactors.exp: Not sanctioned, but severely constrained commercially. Under the January 2025 global settlement with Westinghouse, KHNP is barred for 50 years from bidding nuclear plant projects in North America, the European Union (Czech Republic excepted), the United Kingdom, Japan and Ukraine — which removes most Western SMR markets including Sweden and Norway-adjacent EU business. Permitted markets include the Philippines, Vietnam, Kazakhstan, Morocco, Egypt, Brazil, Argentina, Jordan, Turkey, UAE, Saudi Arabia and South Africa. KHNP also owes roughly $650m of goods/services purchases and $175m of technology licensing fees per exported reactor, and must pass a Westinghouse 'technology independence' verification to independently export next-generation designs — a clause that may be asserted against i-SMR. Korea is an NSG/IAEA-AP state with a US 123 Agreement restricting enrichment and reprocessing.

reactors.ramp_n: IAEA ARIS design status report for i-SMR states load-following capability as '100%-20%-100%, 5%/min'. Vendor states %/min directly; no conversion needed. Meets EUR KP14's 3 %Pr/min. Achieved by reactor power reduction - the i-SMR is a boron-free design and KHNP/KAERI state that soluble-boron adjustment is not needed for daily load following (IAEA catalogue text discusses daily load-following core simulations and radial xenon behaviour).
reactors.minload_n: 20 %Pr, from the same '100%-20%-100%' statement. This is reactor power reduction, not a thermal store or steam bypass, so the reactor genuinely follows load. 20 %Pr matches the level EUR notes may be acceptable for a module.
reactors.auto_n: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 i-SMR entry, Distinguishing features: 'At least 72 hours for core cooling without any safety grade AC/DC power'. The ARIS design status report gives 72 h as the operator-action grace period and ~3 days coping without external support, with passive/air cooling credited beyond that. 'At least' means both are floors. Below EUR KP5's 7-day coping expectation as published; meets the 72 h grace expectation.
reactors.avail_n: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 i-SMR entry: 'the expected available factor no less than 95%'; the ARIS design status report gives 'Lifetime Capacity Factor >95%' with 24-month refuelling staggered across four modules. Vendor-stated (KHNP/KAERI).
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Note KHNP's LARGE reactors EU-APR and APR1000 DID complete EUR assessments (Rev D and Rev E respectively) - those are different designs and must not be credited to i-SMR.

reactors.name: IMSR400 (Integral Molten Salt Reactor)
reactors.fuel: Liquid fluoride fuel salt, UF4 dissolved in fluoride carrier, no cladding; sealed replaceable Core-unit
reactors.fnote: Uses standard-assay LEU (<5% U-235), so no HALEU enrichment bottleneck - a deliberate design choice and the single biggest supply-chain advantage over ThorCon/TMSR-LF1. Critically, IMSR is designed to avoid enriched lithium: IAEA ARIS and World Nuclear Association both describe proprietary non-lithium fluoride diluents, with WNA noting 'initially no Li or Be will be used' though there is 'potential to change to FLiBe'. If the design ever migrates to FLiBe it inherits the full Li-7 problem (see other entries). Remaining gaps are UF4 conversion and fluoride fuel-salt manufacture at commercial scale - there is no merchant MSR fuel-salt supplier anywhere in the West today. DOE Other Transaction Authority 'TEFLA' fuel-line pilot project signed 2026 is intended to close this; Terrestrial also relies on nuclear-grade graphite qualification (irradiation programme ongoing). Enrichment for makeup fuel is quoted in ARIS as 5-19% which would pull it into HALEU territory late in life (vendor claim that first cores run on 2-3%).
reactors.tnote: IAEA ARIS gives 170 t Core-unit transport weight; sealed Core-unit is factory-built, shipped whole and installed in a below-grade silo, then swapped out after ~7 years. 170 t is beyond normal road limits - requires heavy-haul/rail/barge to site. Texas A&M-RELLIS site is inland (Bryan, TX), so heavy-haul road or rail is the assumed route.

lic.s: Vendor Design Review Phase 2 completed - no licence application filed; company has since wound down Canadian project activity
Principal Design Criteria Topical Report approved (safety evaluation issued)
Postulated Initiating Events (PIE) methodology Topical Report approved; no construction permit application submitted as of Q1 2026

reactors.cnote: No nuclear construction. June 2026: signed agreements with the Texas A&M University System for ~77 acres at the Texas A&M-RELLIS campus (Bryan, TX) under ground lease, enabling site characterisation and environmental evaluation ahead of an NRC permit application. Zachry Group engaged under an engineering services agreement. DOE OTA pilots TETRA (reactor) and TEFLA (fuel line) underway. Site work to date is characterisation/survey, not site preparation.
reactors.codnote: Company guides to 'build, license and commission the first IMSR Plants in the early 2030s' (vendor claim). No construction permit application has been filed, so a 2032 COD implies an aggressive NRC schedule; 2034-2035 is the more defensible planning date.

orders.n: MOU announced Q1 2026 targeting up to 4 GW across multiple sites for AI/data-centre load. Non-binding MOU, no unit count, no FID, no deposit disclosed.
Site/ground-lease and R&D agreements at RELLIS campus, June 2026. A siting agreement, not a reactor purchase order.
Collaboration agreement to develop IMSR plant projects for customised energy supply. Development collaboration only.

reactors.health: Strongest balance sheet of the six. Completed SPAC merger with HCM II Acquisition Corp and began trading on Nasdaq under ticker IMSR on 29 October 2025 (~USD 280M gross). Q1 2026 results (14 May 2026): USD 289.9M cash and investments, quarterly burn USD 7.9M, net loss USD 10.5M, total liabilities USD 6.6M - roughly 9 years of runway at current burn, though burn will rise sharply once licensing and long-lead procurement start. Materially de-risked versus Moltex and Saltfoss. Note the strategic pivot: Canada's CEDAR review (March 2026) records that Terrestrial received CAD 25.03M in Canadian federal funding 2016-2023 but ceased Canadian project operations after 2023 and its 2026 shareholder communications contain no Canadian IMSR news - the company is now effectively a US developer with a Canadian corporate history.
reactors.risks: No construction permit application filed anywhere - only topical reports approved, which is early-stage NRC engagement. CNSC VDR Phase 2 left unresolved issues on reactor control and shutdown and on passive safety system effectiveness. Commercial pipeline is entirely non-binding MOUs (Riot 4 GW is a headline number, not an order). Seven-year sealed Core-unit replacement creates a large recurring spent-core logistics and waste stream with no licensed disposition path. Fluoride fuel-salt and nuclear-grade graphite supply chains do not exist commercially. Post-SPAC equity story is exposed to sentiment reversal in the nuclear/AI-power trade. AUDIT: heaviest-module mass unsourced; continuous online fuel addition not explicitly confirmed by the vendor.

reactors.name: KP-FHR (Hermes, Hermes 2, KP-X / KP-150 commercial plant)
reactors.coolant: Flibe (2LiF-BeF2) molten fluoride salt, near-atmospheric pressure
reactors.fuel: TRISO annular pebble fuel — thousands of TRISO particles in a graphite matrix pebble, circulated through the Flibe core
reactors.fnote: Kairos fabricates its own pebbles in-house in partnership with Los Alamos National Laboratory rather than relying on a third-party TRISO vendor — a differentiator, but at laboratory/pilot scale only. DOE finalised the HALEU allocation contract for the Hermes 1 first fuel load on 23 Jan 2026 (material from NNSA sources, 5–20% U-235); quantity undisclosed and it covers Hermes 1 only. Kairos states it can operate on LEU+ until HALEU is broadly available (vendor claim). No commercial-scale pebble line and no secured HALEU stream for Hermes 2 or the commercial fleet has been announced.
reactors.tnote: Kairos uses factory-fabricated modules assembled on site (316H stainless steel vessel, Ibiden ET-10 graphite). Module weights, dimensions and shipping class are not published in the primary sources reviewed; the Oak Ridge site is rail- and barge-accessible. transport_class assigned as heavy_lift by inference, not from a vendor statement.

lic.s: Hermes 1 (35 MWt test reactor, non-power) construction permit CPTR-6 issued — first non-water-cooled reactor approved for construction in the US in over 50 years
Hermes 2 construction permits issued (dockets 05000611 and 05000612), 2 × 35 MWt with power conversion — first electricity-producing Gen IV reactor permitted in the US
Hermes 1 construction permit amendment — latest date for completion of construction extended from 31 Dec 2026 to 30 Apr 2029 (amendment issued 13 May 2026)
Operating licence applications for Hermes 1 and Hermes 2 not yet submitted as of Aug 2026

reactors.cnote: Hermes 1: ground broken July 2024; nuclear (safety-related) construction started May 2025; described by Kairos as the only Gen IV reactor under active nuclear construction in the US, with foundation work progressing. The NRC's May 2026 extension of the construction-completion deadline to April 2029 is a concrete indicator of schedule slip against the original 2026 date. Hermes 2: groundbreaking 17 Apr 2026, foundation work now under way for both units at the Oak Ridge Heritage Center site. DOE ARDP support of up to $303M for the Hermes programme.
reactors.codnote: Kairos states both Hermes facilities are 'expected to be operational before the end of the decade'; the TVA/Google arrangement is reported with a Hermes 2 commercial operation date of 2030. Hermes 1 has an NRC construction-completion backstop of 30 Apr 2029. Commercial KP-150 / KP-X plants follow after Hermes 2. Hermes 2 electrical output is reported as ~50 MWe against an NRC-permitted 2 × 35 MWt — these figures are inconsistent and should be treated as unresolved; the 75 MWe/unit figure used here is the commercial-unit rating from Kairos and the 190 MWt thermal rating is an estimate at ~40% efficiency, not a published number.

orders.n: Commitment to procure up to 500 MW of KP-FHR capacity by 2035 — the first US corporate advanced-reactor 'orderbook'. Unit count not fixed; no per-plant FID.

First US utility PPA for Gen IV output: TVA buys Hermes 2 electricity at market-based time-of-day fixed rates to serve Google data centres in TN and AL. Hermes 2 (2 reactor units) is funded and under construction, so treated as committed.

reactors.health: Private, well-capitalised and technically credible, but no independently verified 2026 financial disclosures were obtainable in this research (no public filings; funding data only via paywalled private-market trackers). Backed by DOE ARDP (up to $303M for Hermes) and by Google's 500 MW offtake commitment plus a TVA PPA. Kairos has an iterative hardware-demonstration culture (non-nuclear ETU test units, in-house salt and pebble manufacturing, Albuquerque manufacturing operations). Treat vendor_health as 'good but unverified' — this is the weakest-evidence field in this record.
reactors.risks: Schedule slip is already documented — NRC extended the Hermes 1 construction-completion deadline by ~2.3 years to April 2029. Neither Hermes has an operating licence application filed yet, so an entire licensing stage remains. Flibe chemistry is the core technical risk: tritium generation and capture from lithium/beryllium, redox control, salt purity, 316H corrosion at 650 °C, and beryllium industrial hygiene. Steam-cycle conditions are not published, so the process-heat and steam-quality proposition cannot be screened quantitatively (steam_temp_c/steam_pressure_bar left null rather than guessed). The mwth_module figure of 190 is an ESTIMATE, not a published rating. Fuel scale-up from in-house lab pebble production to fleet volumes is unproven and HALEU is secured only for Hermes 1. Air-cooling capability and EPZ distance are not established in the sources reviewed — air_cooling_capable set false as unverified rather than as a design limitation. AUDIT: per-module thermal power is inferred from 75 MWe at assumed efficiency, not published by Kairos.

reactors.name: LDR-50 (heat-only district heating reactor)
reactors.fuel: Standard commercial PWR UO2 fuel assemblies; partial reload of 8 assemblies at each outage
reactors.fnote: Standard PWR UO2 at only ~3% U-235 — the lowest enrichment in this screening set, a direct consequence of the low power density and low-temperature duty. Steady Energy states uranium will be sourced from suppliers in friendly countries (Kazakhstan, Australia, Namibia, Canada) with conventional Western conversion/enrichment/fabrication (vendor claim). Essentially zero fuel-supply risk; a partial 8-assembly reload every ~2 years also means very small annual fuel demand per unit.
reactors.tnote: Reactor module described by the vendor as 'roughly the size of an upright city bus' / 'the size of a shipping container', with the core itself about the size of a large washing machine; the whole plant is 'roughly the size of a metro station' on a small-to-medium industrial lot, and the module sits underground and is invisible in the cityscape (vendor claim). Road-transportable by design — the low pressure (<10 bar) permits a thin-walled, light vessel rather than a heavy forging. No module weights published.

lic.s: Concept assessment completed with a positive conclusion — nuclear and radiation safety, security, emergency arrangements and safeguards solutions 'can be designed to meet safety requirements'. This is a pre-licensing procedure, separate from and not equivalent to a construction permit.

lic.j: Multinational joint early review (STUK-FI, SUJB/SSTC NRS/SURO-CZ, PAA-PL, SSM-SE, SNRIU-UA)
lic.s: Report published. Strengths noted in defence-in-depth and passive safety; concept judged 'largely appropriate, but not yet sufficient from a licensing perspective'; crucially, NO regulator identified fundamental obstacles to further development. Significantly more detailed safety analyses, emergency procedures and environmental assessments required for actual licensing.
Reactor design assessment ongoing; no construction licence application submitted

reactors.cnote: No nuclear construction. IMPORTANT DISTINCTION: first concrete was poured on 12 February 2026 at the decommissioned Salmisaari B coal power station in central Helsinki, but this is a NON-NUCLEAR pilot — a 1:1 full-scale replica of the LDR-50 module that uses an electric resistance heater instead of nuclear fuel to simulate decay heat, producing ~6 MW of byproduct heat fed into Helen's district heating network. Its purpose is to demonstrate that the passive safety features behave as designed and to establish supply chains; it is the first full-scale physical test of the module beyond simulation. The lease with Helen runs to 2028. It carries no nuclear licence and is not a nuclear construction precedent.
reactors.codnote: Steady Energy targets a 'ready-to-build' design by 2028, start of construction of the first commercial (nuclear) plant in 2029, and commercial deployment in the early 2030s (vendor claim). No construction licence application has been filed with STUK, and the July 2026 multinational review explicitly found the concept 'not yet sufficient from a licensing perspective', so 2030 should be treated as the optimistic bound; early-to-mid 2030s is the realistic band.

orders.n: Preliminary/conditional agreements for up to 15 reactors in Finland, involving municipal energy companies including Helen (Helsinki), Kuopion Energia and other municipalities assessing nuclear district heating. All are pre-FID feasibility/cooperation agreements, not financed orders.
Host of the Salmisaari non-nuclear pilot (lease to 2028) and takes the pilot's byproduct heat; Helen has launched its own nuclear programme. Not yet a reactor order.
Exclusive operation and maintenance services agreement for Finland and Sweden — a credibility-enhancing partnership with an experienced nuclear operator, not an order.
Sales activity and an MoU regarding deployment in Germany; district heating networks in Poland and Sweden are the main export targets. Nothing contracted.

reactors.health: Venture-stage but credible for its niche. Completed a €32m round on 1 July 2025 (Tesi/Finnish Industry Investment, LocalTapiola, Move Energy, Valo Ventures, 92 Capital) after a ~€22m round in March 2025, plus Finnish state pilot funding — roughly €55-60m raised in total. Spun out of VTT with a decade of state-funded R&D behind the design, and has attracted serious industrial partners (Tractebel for engineering/licensing, Fortum for O&M). Against ~€100m stated cost per commercial unit (vendor claim), the balance sheet is far short of what commercial deployment requires; further large raises or utility partners are essential. Small team, single product, no nuclear construction experience.
reactors.risks: PRODUCES NO ELECTRICITY — mwe_module is genuinely 0. This is a heat-only machine (~90% of thermal output delivered as usable district heat versus ~37% electrical conversion in a conventional plant, per the vendor), so it cannot be screened against electricity-market metrics at all; its economics live or die on district-heating offtake price, network proximity and the willingness of municipalities to site a reactor inside a city. That siting requirement makes public acceptance and a very small emergency planning zone existential rather than merely advantageous — and no regulator has yet granted a reduced EPZ, so epj/epz_km is null, not zero. Licensing is the binding constraint: the July 2026 multinational review found no fundamental obstacles but explicitly judged the concept insufficient for licensing as it stands, and no construction licence application exists. The Salmisaari pilot is electrically heated and proves mechanical/thermal-hydraulic behaviour only, not nuclear performance. Funding is small relative to need. Values entered as derived rather than published: max_process_heat_c (150 C, bounded by the ~155 C outlet — this design cannot serve industrial steam above that), load_following ('excellent' inferred from heat-load duty and low power density, not vendor-verified), air_cooling_capable (true in the sense that all heat is rejected to the DH network, so no condenser cooling water is needed — the parameter is arguably not meaningful for a heat-only plant), and thermal_storage set to 'none' as no storage is integral to the design, though host DH networks typically have accumulators.
reactors.exp: None. Finnish/EU design under Euratom and IAEA safeguards, using ~3% LEU from Western suppliers; no sanctions, no NSG sensitivity, no political-availability constraints. Freely exportable within the EU and to allied markets — cross-border deployment is limited only by each country's willingness to license a novel reactor concept, which is why the multinational joint early review with Czech, Polish, Swedish and Ukrainian regulators matters commercially.

reactors.ramp_n: Not applicable as published, and no number found. The LDR-50 is a 50 MWth district-HEATING reactor with no electrical output, so a %Pr/min electrical ramp is not a meaningful vendor attribute; EUR KP14's %Pr/min would have to be reinterpreted against thermal output. VTT's LDR-50 introduction says the reactor is 'Designed for base-load and load-follow operation' but gives no rate. Load-follow simulations using the VTT Kraken framework exist in the literature (INIS) but are research results, not vendor or regulator statements.
reactors.minload_n: Not published. Same heat-only caveat as above.
reactors.auto_n: Only an imprecise duration is published. Steady Energy / LDR-Reactor FAQ: 'The capacity of the reactor pool is sufficient for receiving heat for several weeks without any cooling.' VTT introduction: 'The pool can receive decay heat for several weeks without any cooling or operator action.' 'Several weeks' clearly exceeds EUR KP5's 72 h and 7 days, but it is a range word, not a number, so I have not converted it. Finland's STUK completed a preliminary assessment of the concept and an international safety review was completed, but neither published a grace or coping figure I could locate.
reactors.avail_n: No availability or capacity factor figure published by Steady Energy.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Steady Energy's own commentary on European nuclear policy discusses EU-level SMR policy, not an EUR assessment. Being a Finnish/European design is not evidence.
