reactors.name: LFR-AS-200 (with LFR-AS-30 demonstrator)
reactors.fuel: MOX (U-Pu mixed oxide) pins, intended to be made from reprocessed plutonium and depleted uranium; closed fuel cycle is the core value proposition
reactors.fnote: Not enriched uranium at all - the design runs on MOX with roughly 20% fissile plutonium content, so 'HALEU' here denotes fissile-equivalent class rather than U-235 enrichment; enrichment_pct is an indicative fissile fraction, not a confirmed specification. The fuel strategy is the company's biggest single vulnerability: the UK government decided to immobilise its 140-tonne separated plutonium stockpile rather than make it available to newcleo, which directly triggered the UK retrenchment in July 2025. newcleo planned its own MOX fabrication plant in France; no plant is operating and no plutonium feedstock is secured. Refuelling interval of ~5 years is an estimate - newcleo has not published a confirmed cycle length.
reactors.tnote: Lead-cooled primary vessel with a lead inventory of several thousand tonnes is inherently a site-assembled heavy-lift item; the LFR-AS-30 demonstrator is smaller. No transport data published.

lic.s: LFR-AS-200 applied for Generic Design Assessment Feb 2024 and was accepted into GDA in June 2025 - but newcleo announced on 31 July 2025 that it was scaling back UK operations (from ~150 staff to a minimal presence), so GDA progress is in question.
Regulatory Justification application submitted April 2024

Pre-licensing dialogue opened 2023, preparatory stages completed February 2024, for the 30 MWe LFR-AS-30 demonstrator at Chinon (land acquisition initiated Feb 2025). No construction licence application.

reactors.cnote: No nuclear construction. The only hardware is 'Precursor', a NON-NUCLEAR electrically heated mockup rated 10 MW thermal with ~3 MW power conversion, due to complete by end-2026 at ENEA's Brasimone Research Centre in Italy. Do not read this as a reactor build.
reactors.codnote: Published targets are a 30 MWe LFR-AS-30 pilot in France around 2030-2031 and 200 MWe commercial deployment in the UK by 2033 (vendor claim). Given the going-concern qualification, the UK retrenchment and no licence application in any jurisdiction, these dates should be treated as aspirational; NucNet still classifies the design as conceptual.

orders.n: January 2025 joint venture for up to four LFR-AS-200 units at the Jaslovske Bohunice V1 site. Non-binding, no FID, no financing.

orders.c: NextChem / MAIRE (Next-N JV), Danieli, Cementir, Walter Tosto, Orion Valves
orders.n: Industrial shareholders and a JV rather than customers; these are supply-chain and equity relationships, not reactor orders.

reactors.health: WEAK - the clear outlier on financial risk. PwC issued a going-concern warning on 5 August 2025, flagging 'substantial uncertainty' and 'significant doubts' about newcleo's ability to continue operations absent confirmed new capital: 2024 loss of EUR 110M (double the prior year), EUR 13M/month cash burn, net liquidity down to EUR 160M at 25 April 2025 from EUR 282M at end-2023, personnel costs EUR 69M. Response was a conservative plan - reduced hiring, scaled-back investment, and halting UK operations. Subsequent raises were modest relative to burn: EUR 75M and an $85M round closed February 2026 (Kairos, Indaco, Azimut, CERN pension fund, Walter Tosto returning; Danieli, Cementir, Orion Valves and NextChem new), bringing total raised to over $755M since 2021 with only ~$125M in the preceding twelve months. Against a historical EUR 13M/month burn that is roughly a year of runway, and far short of the 'up to EUR 3bn of French investment by 2030' once announced. CEO Stefano Buono is now redirecting toward US market entry.
reactors.risks: Financial viability is the primary screening risk - a formal auditor going-concern qualification, heavy burn against modest raises, and a strategic retreat from the UK after losing access to the plutonium stockpile. Fuel cycle risk is existential to the business case: no MOX feedstock secured, no fabrication plant, and the closed-cycle premise depends on government plutonium policy that has already gone against them once. Technically, lead corrosion/erosion, the 530C outlet with lead chemistry control, and seismic qualification of a heavy lead-filled vessel are all unresolved at scale. No construction, no licence application, no FID customer, and the only hardware is a non-nuclear mockup. Strategy is also unsettled - Italy, France, UK, Slovakia and now the US, with capital spread thin.

The design is at conceptual stage with no completed regulatory review, so no regulator-confirmed value exists. Not converted.

reactors.name: MMR / KRONOS MMR (formerly Ultra Safe Nuclear Micro Modular Reactor)
reactors.fuel: Fully Ceramic Microencapsulated (FCM) fuel — annular cylindrical pellets of TRISO particles in a SiC ceramic matrix, in prismatic graphite blocks
reactors.fnote: Weakest fuel position of the five. In the USNC bankruptcy the FUEL business was sold separately from the reactor IP: Standard Nuclear Inc. bought USNC's fuel assets (FCM/TRISO manufacturing, Oak Ridge base) for $28M (auction Oct 2024, closed Feb 2025), while NANO Nuclear bought only the MMR and Pylon reactor IP. NANO therefore owns the reactor design but not the fuel line that was developed for it, and must contract fuel supply and secure HALEU. NANO is standing up its own fuel capability, but no qualified FCM production line and no announced HALEU allocation exist as of Aug 2026. NANO cites a 9.9–20% enrichment range for KRONOS (vendor claim).
reactors.tnote: Vendor describes a modular system 'capable of being transported by road and assembled on site', with plant separation into a Nuclear Plant (reactor units) and an Adjacent Plant (power conversion), so the nuclear island ships as road-legal modules (vendor claim). No published module weights.

lic.s: Construction permit application submitted by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign for a 45 MWth KRONOS MMR on campus (Champaign County, IL)
Acceptance review completed / application formally docketed for review. NRC milestones: draft safety evaluation and draft environmental assessment Feb 2027, final EA May 2027, final SER Sept 2027

Legacy Global First Power MMR project at Chalk River — licence-to-prepare-site review; NANO acquired Global First Power from USNC and expects 'further demonstrations' pending Canadian government approvals. Status effectively stalled/inherited rather than advancing.

reactors.cnote: No construction anywhere. NANO expects an approximately 12-month NRC review of the UIUC application and states construction activities could 'initiate in mid-late 2027'. The design has never been built; USNC's Chalk River MMR never reached construction before the bankruptcy.
reactors.codnote: Nominal — derived from NANO's stated mid-to-late 2027 construction start plus a first-of-a-kind build and commissioning period; NANO has not published a committed COD. Treat as low confidence. The 240-month (20-year) refuel interval reflects the MMR's whole-core cartridge concept and was NOT confirmed in the primary sources reviewed in this research — verify before using.

orders.n: UIUC is the NRC applicant (not NANO); research/demonstration deployment on campus. Collaboration extended Jan 2026. No commercial FID.
Contract award announced Sept 2025 for KRONOS MMR work; scope is developmental, not a reactor purchase.

orders.c: Supermicro / EHC Investment (Gulf region JV) / DS Dansuk (South Korea, Asia localisation)
orders.n: Three MoUs announced in NANO's Q2 FY2026 update — non-binding, exploratory.

reactors.health: CRITICAL HISTORY: the original developer, Ultra Safe Nuclear Corporation (Seattle), filed Chapter 11 on 30 Oct 2024 in Delaware together with subsidiaries USNC-Technologies, USNC-Power and Global First Power, explicitly to facilitate a sale. The estate was split: NANO Nuclear Energy agreed on 24 Dec 2024 to acquire the MMR and Pylon reactor IP (~38 issued/pending patents), contracts and worldwide demonstration partnerships for $8.5M, closing 24 Dec 2024, and separately acquired Global First Power; Standard Nuclear Inc. (CEO Dr Kurt Terrani, ex-USNC VP; backed by Decisive Point, Andreessen Horowitz, Crucible Capital, Fundomo, Washington Harbour Partners, $42M round) bought the FUEL assets for $28M, closing Feb 2025. NANO rebranded MMR as KRONOS MMR and Pylon as LOKI MMR (Jan 2025). NANO itself is now well funded: $568.7M cash and short-term investments at 31 Mar 2026, only $9.3M used in operating activities over six months, plus $900M shelf and a $400M ATM. So: dead original vendor, healthy acquirer balance sheet, but a discontinuity in engineering team, fuel supply and project continuity.
reactors.risks: Highest institutional-discontinuity risk of the five. The design changed owners through a bankruptcy, and the fuel business went to a DIFFERENT buyer (Standard Nuclear) than the reactor IP (NANO) — so the reactor developer does not control its own fuel. No HALEU allocation announced. No unit has ever been built; the Chalk River project that was the original lead deployment stalled with USNC's collapse. The NRC applicant is a university, not a utility, so the first project has no commercial revenue model and limited nuclear project-execution depth. NANO is a small-cap listed company with a large cash pile but no delivery track record. Power rating is variable in vendor material (10–45 MWth / 3.5–15 MWe range; the UIUC unit is 45 MWth) — figures used here are the top of the range. The 20-year refuelling interval and air-cooling ('operates without water requirements', vendor claim) need independent verification. Steam conditions are not published (helium/salt outlet ~660 °C, with a claimed 950 °C future variant that is concept-level only).

reactors.ramp_n: No rate published. The IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 MMR entry does not state a load-following rate; NANO Nuclear (which acquired the USNC MMR technology and rebranded it KRONOS MMR) has not published one either. The KRONOS MMR construction permit application submitted by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign to the NRC is for a research/demonstration unit.
reactors.minload_n: Not published. The MMR is described as a 'flexible nuclear battery' but with no minimum power figure; in the MMR architecture, output flexibility is intended to come from the molten-salt intermediate heat-storage loop and the balance of plant rather than from reactor power reduction, so the reactor would not follow load - but the vendor does not quantify this.
reactors.auto_n: Only unquantified claims. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024, MMR entry: 'The MMR reactor is designed to ensure safety without relying on active or powered systems, or operator actions'; 'no operator action is required during abnormal or accident conditions'; 'The MMR has been designed to ensure that the reactor can manage Design Basis Conditions (DBC) without the need for electrical power, engineered control actions, or operator intervention.' No hour or day figure is attached, and no NRC-confirmed value exists yet. Not converted into a number.
reactors.avail_n: No availability or capacity factor percentage published.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Out of EUR SMLWR scope in any case (gas-cooled micro reactor).

reactors.name: Natrium (Kemmerer Unit 1)
reactors.vendor: TerraPower (with GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy)
reactors.coolant: Liquid sodium (pool-type primary), intermediate sodium loop, nitrate molten-salt thermal store
reactors.fuel: Sodium-bonded metallic U-Zr (U-10Zr) alloy pins with HT9 ferritic-martensitic cladding
reactors.fnote: Four-track HALEU strategy: Centrus enrichment at Piketon OH (Centrus hit its 900 kg Phase 2 DOE milestone in Jan 2026 and won a $900M DOE award), Framatome metallization pilot in Richland WA, Global Nuclear Fuel-Americas fabrication in Wilmington NC, plus an ASP Isotopes long-term supply agreement targeted operational by 2028. HALEU availability was the single named cause of the 2028->2030 schedule slip. No commercial-scale metallic HALEU fuel fabrication line is yet qualified and operating, so fuel remains the binding constraint. Enrichment stated as HALEU below 20%; 19.75% is the design ceiling rather than a confirmed core average.
reactors.tnote: Large reactor vessel and guard vessel are heavy-lift items; Kemmerer site was chosen partly for rail access to a retiring coal plant. Component module weights not published.

lic.s: 10 CFR Part 50 construction permit issued (final safety evaluation Dec 2025; Commission authorization 4 March 2026) - first US non-LWR construction permit in over 40 years. Operating licence application still to come (expected ~Feb 2031).
Generic Design Assessment Step 1 commenced; design accepted into GDA Feb 2026, Step 1 start 17 June 2026

reactors.cnote: Non-nuclear energy island works started June 2024. Nuclear-island construction formally commenced 23 April 2026 following the March 2026 construction permit; ~1,600 construction workers, ~250 permanent staff. Approximately 36 months from nuclear concrete to fuel load. Total project cost ~$4bn, roughly 50/50 DOE ARDP cost-share and private capital.
reactors.codnote: TerraPower targets 2030, with sources indicating a 2030-2031 window and an operating-licence application around Feb 2031; original target was 2028 and slipped on HALEU availability. Treat 2031 as the realistic case.

orders.n: First unit under construction at the retiring Naughton coal plant site in Kemmerer, Wyoming; PacifiCorp has studied additional units in its IRP but has not committed.

Agreement announced 9 Jan 2026: early development activities for two units plus rights to energy from up to six more; up to 2.8 GW baseload / 4 GW peak. No site selected at announcement, first units 'as early as 2032'. Not an FID (vendor claim on capacity figures).

reactors.health: Strong. Privately held, Bill Gates-founded; $650M raise closed June 2025 with NVIDIA's NVentures joining alongside Gates and HD Hyundai; ~$2bn DOE ARDP cost-share. First-mover position validated by the NRC construction permit. Main exposure is single-project concentration and fuel-supply timing rather than balance sheet.
reactors.risks: HALEU supply chain is the dominant risk - no qualified commercial metallic HALEU fabrication line yet operating; FOAK cost and schedule on a first-of-a-kind sodium plant with a novel salt-storage energy island; sodium handling and steam-generator (salt-to-steam) commissioning risk; Meta agreement is pre-FID with no site; only one construction permit in hand, so fleet economics unproven. AUDIT: air-cooling capability for the power island is not confirmed by TerraPower.

reactors.ramp_n: No rate published, and the question is structurally different for this design. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 Natrium entry: 'The Natrium reactor maintains its thermal reactor power constant during its entire operating period, eliminating reactor power cycling and maximizing its capacity factor and value.' Plant electrical output varies via the molten-salt thermal energy storage system: nominal 345 MWe, 'can boost output to 500 MWe for more than five and a half hours to serve peak demand', and the store 'can also fully discharge and recharge three times per day'. TerraPower publishes no MW/min or %/min figure, so no conversion is possible - the boost duration alone does not give a rate.
reactors.minload_n: Not published as a number, but the mechanism is explicitly a THERMAL STORE, not reactor power reduction: the reactor runs at constant 840 MWt while the salt store buffers output. The plant therefore follows load while the reactor does not, and any 'minimum load' figure would describe turbine/store dispatch, not reactor stability. TerraPower does not state a minimum plant output.
reactors.auto_n: Only unquantified claims. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 Natrium entry: inherent safety features act 'with no need of operator action, AC power, or control systems'; the design provides 'reliable shut-down with no operator action required'. No hour or day figure is attached. The NRC construction permit review for Kemmerer 1 is under way but I found no published grace/coping duration. Not converted.
reactors.avail_n: No percentage published. The IAEA entry says constant reactor power is 'maximizing its capacity factor' but gives no figure.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Out of EUR SMLWR scope (sodium-cooled fast reactor).

reactors.name: NUWARD SMR (post-2024 reset design)
reactors.vendor: Nuward SAS (EDF subsidiary; CEA, TechnicAtome, Framatome, Tractebel in industrial base)
reactors.coolant: Light water (pressurised, two external primary loops)
reactors.fuel: UO2 pellets in standard Framatome PWR fuel assemblies with shortened rods; fully compatible with existing French fuel-cycle and reprocessing facilities
reactors.fnote: Deliberate design choice after the 2024 reset: standard ~5% LEU UO2 on existing Framatome production lines, recyclable in existing French cycle facilities, enabling 24-month cycles (vendor claim). No new fuel qualification or HALEU dependency — this is the strongest single de-risking feature of the redesign.
reactors.tnote: The reset design abandoned the integral 2x170 MWe concept: steam generators are now external, connected by two primary loops, inside a pre-stressed concrete containment. Consequence for screening: this is NOT a road/rail-transportable modular reactor — RPV and SGs are large forged components requiring barge/heavy-lift delivery. Vendor emphasises maximum prefabrication and highly automated 'Industry 4.0' module factories, 60-month FOAK build and <48 months for follow-on units (vendor claim).

lic.s: JER Phase 3 launched — 8 European regulators; technical meetings held 12 Mar 2026 and 26 Jun 2026. Non-binding; does not substitute for national licensing.

lic.j: Europe (ASN/ASNR-FR, STUK-FI, SUJB-CZ, PAA-PL, SSM-SE, ANVS-NL)
lic.s: JER Phase 2 reports published — but assessed the SUPERSEDED 2x170 MWe integral design, not the current 400 MWe concept
No safety options file (DOS) or construction authorisation application filed for the reset design
Withdrawn — EDF exited the Great British Nuclear SMR competition in July 2024 citing design maturity

reactors.cnote: No site, no licence application, no construction. The programme was reset in July 2024 and formally relaunched in January 2025 (Julien Garrel replaced Renaud Crassous as executive president). The original indigenous integral 2x170 MWe design with in-vessel SGs and compact containment was scrapped as too costly/immature; the replacement is a conventional single-reactor ~400 MWe two-loop PWR built from 'well-known and perfectly mastered technological building blocks'. Candidate French sites (Cordemais, Fessenheim) have expressed interest but none is selected.
reactors.codnote: Conceptual design completion slipped from mid-2026 to end-2026; basic design 2026-2029; detailed design from 2030; construction start ~2030; first unit operating ~2035, with a first fleet of 3-4 reactors in one or two European countries (vendor claim). A 2050 goal of ~30 units has been stated. Treat 2035 as optimistic — this design is at concept stage in 2026 with no licensing docket open.

orders.n: Edison joined the International NUWARD Advisory Board Dec 2025 and has floated two units in the 2030-2040 window; on 25 Jun 2026 NUWARD/EDF signed an industrial Declaration of Intent with 8 Italian companies. Non-binding — no order, no FID.
Technical collaboration agreement Nov 2025 (industrial cogeneration applications). Not an order.

reactors.health: Weak-to-moderate for a programme of this ambition. EDF is 100% French state-owned and carries very high debt with capital priority on the EPR2 fleet; Nuward's original design was written off in 2024 and its leadership replaced. As of July 2026 EDF is actively seeking external European industrial and financial investors for the Nuward subsidiary, targeting a deal by end-2026 — funding for basic/detailed design is NOT secured, and EDF has disclosed neither a valuation nor a target raise. Strong technical backing (Framatome, TechnicAtome, CEA, Tractebel) and explicit French political support (Macron, March 2026).
reactors.risks: Highest schedule/design risk in this set: the design was reset once already and the conceptual phase has slipped. Several parameters here are DERIVED, NOT PUBLISHED — mwth_module (~1200 MWt inferred from 400 MWe at ~33% efficiency), coolant_outlet_c (~310 C typical loop PWR), and load_following (assumed good from EDF grid practice) are not vendor-published and should be re-verified before use. Steam conditions are unpublished. Other risks: no site, no licence docket, financing unsecured, no firm order; the 400 MWe size is at the top of the SMR band and loses the road-transportable/factory-complete value proposition; the JER regulatory work completed so far applies to a design that no longer exists.
reactors.exp: None. French/EU design under Euratom and IAEA safeguards; exports subject to routine NSG/EU dual-use controls. No sanctions or political-availability constraints in Western markets.

reactors.ramp_n: No rate published. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 NUWARD entry states only that 'The design offers baseload and load-following' operation; the 2022 EDF/NUWARD conference presentation says only '60 years of operation load-following capability'. No %/min, MW/min or %/hour figure found from EDF or from the ASN-led Joint Early Review.
reactors.minload_n: Not published. Note NUWARD is boron-free in normal operation and in all Design Basis Conditions (IAEA entry), which usually widens the rod-only manoeuvring band, but EDF publishes no minimum stable power.
reactors.auto_n: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 NUWARD entry: the ultimate heat sink (the reactor pool) 'offers a coping time of more than 3 days without the need for intervention'. I record 3 days / 72 h; the vendor says 'more than', so both numbers are floors, not the actual capability. No 7-day figure and no separate operator-action grace period found. Caveat: EDF fundamentally reset the NUWARD design in July 2024 (moving away from the integrated 2x170 MWe layout toward a simpler ~400 MWe plant), so figures drawn from the pre-2024 design description may not survive into the current one.
reactors.avail_n: Two consistent vendor statements: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 NUWARD entry, 'The design target value for the lifetime capacity factor is above 90%, with the major planned refuelling only outages scheduled for 20 days every 24 months'; and the 2022 EDF/NUWARD presentation, '>90% availability'. Recorded as 90 (a floor). Same 2024 design-reset caveat applies.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments, and no announced EUR assessment found. NUWARD is the test case for the ASN/STUK/Czech SUJB Joint Early Review (phase 2 completed) - that is a multinational REGULATORY review, not an EUR utility-requirements assessment, and must not be scored as one. Being a European design is not evidence of EUR assessment.

reactors.name: PWR-20
reactors.fuel: Standard off-the-shelf LEU UO2 PWR fuel assemblies (existing commercial fuel licences); sealed long-cycle core
reactors.fnote: Explicit product strategy is to use 'off-the-shelf LEU fuel with existing licenses' at <5% enrichment from the incumbent Western fuel vendors (vendor claim). No HALEU, no novel fuel qualification, no new fabrication line — the lowest fuel-supply risk in this screening set alongside i-SMR and LDR-50. Residual question is whether a bespoke small-core assembly geometry is required, which Last Energy has not published.
reactors.tnote: Core proposition is full factory fabrication with road-transportable modules, assembled on site in 6-24 months; nuclear island footprint quoted as ~114 sq ft with the complete modular plant under 0.5 acre (~0.2 ha) (vendor claim). Containment is a double-hermetic-sealed steel vessel inside a ~1,000-tonne concrete vault poured on site. Individual module weights are not published. Air-cooled design requires no large water body (stated in Last Energy's NRC regulatory engagement plan), which is a genuine siting advantage for West Texas data-centre loads.

lic.s: Preliminary Design Review of the PWR-20 completed successfully; entered the Nuclear Site Licensing process Feb 2025; ONR confirmed the December 2027 site-licence decision target is achievable contingent on submission quality

Pre-application engagement only. Regulatory Engagement Plan filed; intends 10 CFR Part 52 pathway with an Early Site Permit for a Texas site; explicitly will NOT submit emergency-planning information with the ESP. No design certification or construction permit application docketed.
Selected for the DOE Nuclear Reactor Pilot Program (Aug 2025) — the PWR-5 test reactor at Texas A&M-RELLIS proceeds under DOE authorisation rather than NRC licensing, targeting criticality in 2026

reactors.cnote: No PWR-20 has been built or is under construction anywhere. The activity in progress is a smaller 5 MWe PWR-5 demonstration unit at the Texas A&M-RELLIS campus in Bryan, Texas under DOE's Reactor Pilot Program, with testing/criticality targeted in 2026 — this is a different, smaller machine and is not a PWR-20 licence precedent. In the UK, the four-unit Llynfi (Bridgend, South Wales) project — 'Prosiect Egni Glan Llynfi', ~£300m, 80 MWe across 4 units, 22 MW grid connection offer secured — is in site licensing and planning; no construction consent, no first concrete.
reactors.codnote: UK site-licence decision targeted December 2027; the original 'first plant in 2027' claim is no longer achievable. Vendor claims fabrication, transport and assembly within 24 months per unit and 6-24 month module deployment (vendor claim), which would put a UK FOAK around 2029-2030 at the earliest even if licensing holds. The 2026 PWR-5 criticality at RELLIS, if achieved, is the key near-term credibility milestone to watch.

orders.c: Llynfi Clean Energy Project (Bridgend, South Wales)
orders.n: 80 MWe on a former coal power station site; £300m stated capex, no public funding; 22 MW grid connection offer secured Jan 2025; $103.7m US EXIM letter of intent Dec 2024. In ONR site licensing + planning. No FID.
600 MWe across 30 units on a 200-acre site; ERCOT interconnection filed; ESP application to NRC in preparation. Announced Feb 2025. No FID, no licence.

orders.c: European industrial / data-centre customers (Poland, UK and others)
orders.n: Company claims ~80 commercial agreements / PPAs across Europe (34 in Poland and the UK were announced earlier), ~40 of them serving data centres (vendor claim). These are conditional offtake agreements, not financed orders — treat the pipeline number as marketing until an FID is announced.

reactors.health: Well-funded for its stage but pre-revenue and unproven. Closed an oversubscribed $100m+ Series C on 16 December 2025 led by the Astera Institute, with JAM Fund, Gigafund, The Haskell Company, AE Ventures, Ultranative, Galaxy Interactive and Woori Technology participating; company states this fully capitalises it through the DOE pilot. Also holds a $103.7m EXIM letter of intent for the Welsh project. Private, venture-backed, has never built or operated a reactor, and is simultaneously pursuing a build-own-operate utility model that is far more capital-intensive than equipment sales. Note it has also publicly campaigned (with Texas and Utah) against NRC microreactor regulation as 'overburdensome' — a signal of regulatory-pathway friction.
reactors.risks: No PWR-20 has been licensed, built, fuelled or operated anywhere; the only near-term hardware is a different, smaller PWR-5. US pathway depends on either DOE authorisation (which does not produce a commercially replicable NRC licence) or an NRC Part 52 route on which only pre-application engagement has occurred. The business model requires a very small EPZ (effectively site-boundary) to site 20 MWe units next to industrial and data-centre loads — Last Energy has explicitly deferred emergency-planning submissions, so this central economic assumption is untested with the NRC; epz_km is therefore null, not small. The advertised 80-plus 'agreements' pipeline is non-binding with zero FIDs. Unverified in this pass: refuel_months (72 reflects the vendor's sealed long-cycle claim, not a published core design), steam conditions, module weights, and load-following capability (set to 'limited' as a conservative default for a small baseload PWR serving data centres). BOO/PPA model concentrates capital, construction, operating and decommissioning risk on a venture-stage balance sheet.
reactors.exp: None restrictive. US design; exports would require standard NRC/DOE Part 810 authorisations and a 123 Agreement with the destination state (both already satisfied for the UK and EU). Freely available to Western and allied markets — the least politically constrained design in this set alongside Nuward and LDR-50.

reactors.avail_n: No PWR-20-specific figure. The '>90% utilization rate' on Last Energy's site refers to the existing global PWR fleet, not to this design, and I have not adopted it.

reactors.name: RITM-200N land-based (Yakutia SNPP) with RITM-200S / KLT-40S floating variants (Akademik Lomonosov, Baimskaya PEB-106)
reactors.fuel: Cermet fuel — uranium dioxide dispersed in an aluminium-silicon (silumin) matrix, marine-heritage assemblies; no soluble-boron control system
reactors.fnote: CRITICAL SCREENING FLAG: RITM-200N/S use sub-20% HALEU cermet fuel ('below 20%' per Rosatom's IAEA INPRO presentation), a fuel form manufactured only by Rosatom (TVEL) for the Russian icebreaker fleet. It is mature and proven inside Russia (score would be 5 domestically) but there is NO non-Russian supply chain, no Western qualification, and no realistic second source — hence a 2 on a global screening basis. Any customer is locked into Rosatom fuel and back-end services for the 60-year plant life. Note also that >5% enrichment triggers separate transport, safeguards and physical-protection regimes in most jurisdictions.
reactors.tnote: Land-based RITM-200N: shop-fabricated modules shipped to site; the steel containment envelope is 8.7 m diameter x 21 m. Ust-Kuyga is reached via the Northern Sea Route and Yana River barge, with ~9,500 t of cargo scheduled per season and a 12 km access road built — logistics, not reactor technology, is the dominant constraint. Floating variants are self-delivering: the whole plant is towed to site (Akademik Lomonosov hull 144 m x 30 m, ~21,500 t; Baimskaya PEB-106 hulls, Project 20871). Module weights not published.

lic.s: Siting licence for Yakutia SNPP unit 1 (2023); construction licence granted April 2023; Rosprirodnadzor construction permit for the first 55 MWe RITM-200N unit May 2024. Final detailed design completed June 2022.
Fully licensed and in commercial operation (Akademik Lomonosov, Pevek) since May 2020
Construction under way — first structural concrete for the SMR reactor building poured March 2026
None — no pre-application, no GDA, and no realistic pathway

reactors.cnote: STATUS DIFFERS BY VARIANT — do not read a single value. (a) RITM-200N land-based, Ust-Kuyga, Yakutia: construction licence held since April 2023, worker camps and 12 km access road built, long-lead forgings and stainless blanks in production since Dec 2023, but the EPC schedule (ASE) places main production buildings and principal construction-assembly works in 2026-2027 — i.e. still early works, first structural concrete for the reactor building not confirmed. Scope was raised in June 2024 from one to two units (110 MWe total). (b) Floating KLT-40S: Akademik Lomonosov (2 x 35 MWe) has been in commercial operation at Pevek since May 2020, passed 1 billion kWh in January 2025 and completed its first full refuelling in January 2025 — this is the only SMR in the world with a multi-year commercial operating record. (c) Modernised floating units: the first RITM-200S reactor for the Baimskaya PEB-106 fleet was completed at ZiO-Podolsk on 28 May 2026; four hulls (three operating + one rotating spare) are under construction. (d) Export: Uzbekistan Jizzakh SMR poured first concrete March 2026 — but scope was cut from six RITM-200N units to two.
reactors.codnote: Yakutia RITM-200N unit 1 target remains 2028 (Rosatom, restated consistently since 2023) — treat as at risk given main construction works are only scheduled for 2026-2027 and the site is Arctic with a short delivery season. First Baimskaya floating unit commissioning 2028, full mine power ~2029. Uzbekistan first SMR criticality late 2029 (revised). Akademik Lomonosov: already operating (COD May 2020).

orders.n: 110 MWe total (2 x 55 MWe RITM-200N). State-funded, licensed, under construction. Anchor load is the Kyuchus gold deposit (Seligdar/Rostec cluster).

First-ever overseas Russian SMR. Contract signed 2024 originally for six 55 MWe RITM-200N units (330 MWe); REDUCED to two units, with two VVER-1000s added to the site. First concrete March 2026; first SMR criticality late 2029.

Four floating power units (Project 20871 / PEB-106), each 2 x RITM-200S = 106 MWe; three operating plus one rotating spare. First RITM-200S reactor manufactured 28 May 2026; first FPU commissioning 2028. Hull construction partly at Chinese shipyards.
Operating floating plant, 2 x KLT-40S = 70 MWe plus up to ~50 Gcal/h district heat; replaced the retiring Bilibino EGP-6 units.

orders.c: Kazakhstan, Iran, Myanmar, Ethiopia, Burkina Faso (talks)
orders.n: Early-stage discussions only; no binding SMR contracts. OSW notes Rosatom has signed no new binding export contracts in roughly five years.

reactors.health: Financially robust but strategically constrained. Rosatom revenue has grown since 2022 on overseas construction, it retains ~15% of EU and a large share of US enrichment supply, and it escaped comprehensive Western sanctions. However it faces payment-settlement and logistics frictions that are causing schedule slippage across its portfolio (Akkuyu, Paks II, El Dabaa), lost Hanhikivi outright, is effectively excluded from all future Western projects, and its ability to co-finance projects depends on a Russian state budget under war-related strain. It also faces growing Chinese competition. Technically, OKBM Afrikantov's RITM line is the most operationally proven SMR reactor family in the world (icebreaker fleet plus Akademik Lomonosov), with eight RITM reactors reported in production simultaneously.
reactors.risks: Geopolitical availability is the dominant risk and dwarfs technical risk (see export_restrictions). Technical/commercial risks: HALEU cermet fuel is single-sourced from Rosatom for the plant's 60-year life; the land-based RITM-200N is still a FOAK adaptation of a marine reactor with no operating land unit anywhere; Arctic construction logistics drive both schedule and cost; the Uzbekistan scope cut from six units to two is a negative signal on SMR economics/confidence. Unverified values in this record: coolant_outlet_c (318 C) and steam parameters are marine RITM-200 figures, not RITM-200N-specific published data — one IAEA INPRO slide deck reads '1,190 MWt' which is a transcription artefact of 190 MWt. epz_km entered as 0 because Rosatom states the protective buffer stays within the SNPP site boundary; this is a design claim (vendor claim) not an approved regulatory determination in any Western jurisdiction. air_cooling_capable set false — not verified either way.
reactors.exp: Most restricted design in this set. Rosatom itself has largely avoided blanket sanctions, but: (1) the US prohibits imports of Russian uranium products (waivers expiring, hard cut-off from 2028) and Russia has imposed retaliatory enriched-uranium export restrictions on the US; (2) the EU is legislating an end to Russian nuclear fuel and service imports and annulled state-aid approval for Paks II in September 2025; (3) US, EU, UK, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia and most of the OECD are closed to new Rosatom projects as a matter of policy — Rosatom is 'effectively excluded from any future involvement in new projects on Western markets'; (4) banking, insurance and shipping frictions delay even permitted projects; (5) HALEU (<20%) fuel adds NSG/IAEA safeguards, transport and physical-protection burdens on top. Realistically available markets are Central Asia (Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan), parts of Africa, Iran, Myanmar and other states willing to accept Russian state financing and a full fuel-cycle dependency. For any Western, EU, UK, Japanese, Korean or US-aligned buyer, treat this design as unavailable regardless of technical merit.

reactors.name: Rolls-Royce SMR
reactors.coolant: Light water (three-loop PWR with conventional forced circulation, boron-free reactivity control in normal operation)
reactors.fuel: UO2 in standard 17x17 lattice assemblies derived from the Westinghouse RFA design (264 fuel rods, 24 guide thimbles, 1 instrument tube), 121 assemblies, gadolinia-doped burnable absorbers
reactors.fnote: GDA E3S Case Chapter 4 confirms a maximum enrichment of 4.95 w% U-235 for undoped fuel and an 18-month three-batch equilibrium cycle. The assembly geometry is conventional so multiple Western fabricators could supply, but the boron-free core relies on heavy gadolinia doping and grey-rod control, and no UK supply route (Springfields) has been contracted and qualified for this specific product. Design-specific fuel qualification is still outstanding.
reactors.tnote: Design intent is that the entire power station is built from around 1,500 factory-manufactured, transportable modules in three families: heavy pressure vessels, MEP modules, and civil/structural modules - all sized for conventional road transport in the UK (vendor claim). Heaviest single module mass is not published. RPV manufacture was outsourced to third-party forgers (Doosan Enerbility and Skoda JS selected May 2026 for nuclear island components), and the largest vessels realistically move by sea plus abnormal-load road haul.

lic.s: GDA Step 3 (detailed assessment) in progress since 31 Jul 2024, following the Step 2 GDA statement of Jul 2024. GDA is expected to conclude by December 2026 with DAC/SoDA. This is the furthest any SMR design has progressed through a European regulatory assessment.

Wylfa (Ynys Mon) site-specific design and regulatory engagement under the Great British Energy - Nuclear contract signed 13 Apr 2026; nuclear site licence application still ahead. ONR has established Wylfa SMR project communications.
Early works contract with CEZ for up to 3 GW at the Temelin site; site-specific design and licensing activities under way

reactors.cnote: No nuclear construction. The Wylfa contract signed 13 Apr 2026 secures 'contractual certainty' and unlocks site-specific design, but a final investment decision is a separate later milestone widely reported as expected around 2029. The Sheffield AMRC Module Development Facility (initial GBP 2.7m, wider GBP 15m+ package) is building prototype modules, not plant. The vendor's 500-day build target and 4-year overall programme (2 years site prep, 2 years construction and commissioning) are unvalidated (vendor claim).
reactors.codnote: Rolls-Royce SMR states first commercial unit in the early 2030s (vendor claim); UK Government messaging for Wylfa points to grid connection in the mid-2030s, and with FID not expected until around 2029 a 2035 first COD is the realistic screening assumption.

orders.c: Great British Energy - Nuclear (Wylfa, Ynys Mon)
orders.n: Contract signed 13 Apr 2026 for at least 1,400 MW; GBP 3.4bn allocated by UK Government to the contract and wider programme, plus a National Wealth Fund loan facility (reported at up to GBP 599m by the vendor and up to GBP 810m in some accounts) to complete the generic design. Firm contract but FID still ahead, reported as expected around 2029.
Early works contract for up to 3 GW (~6 units). CEZ also holds a 20% equity stake in Rolls-Royce SMR, acquired Oct 2024, so this is a shareholder-linked order.
Selected Jun 2026 to deliver up to 1,500 MWe. Selection only, no FID.
Shortlisted alongside BWRX-300.

orders.c: Various (Poland, Finland, Turkey, Estonia, Netherlands, Ukraine)
orders.n: Memoranda of understanding only.

reactors.health: Solid and improving, but still pre-revenue and dependent on public money. Rolls-Royce SMR Limited is a subsidiary of Rolls-Royce plc (LSE: RR, which itself has recovered strongly since 2023) with CEZ Group holding 20% since Oct 2024 and legacy stakes held by the Perrodo family, Qatar and Constellation Energy. Cumulative public and private funding exceeds GBP 1 billion (GBP 210m UK Government and GBP 195m private in 2021, plus a National Wealth Fund loan facility of up to ~GBP 599m in Apr 2026). The Apr 2026 Wylfa contract with GBP 3.4bn of allocated Government funding materially de-risks the near term. Roughly 600 staff across Derby, Warrington and Manchester as of the last public figure. No distress or layoffs identified. Structural risk is concentration: the company's viability is tied to a single sovereign programme.
reactors.risks: At 470 MWe this is not a small SMR - it is a mid-size PWR, which undercuts the 'factory-built, truck-delivered' modularity story and puts it in direct competition with conventional large PWRs on cost per kW. The 21,500 m2 (5.3 acre) footprint figure is the power-island assembly area, not the licensed site: Wikipedia and other sources cite ~10 acres (4 ha) for the site, so treat footprint_ha as the vendor's compact-site claim. Boron-free operation with grey-rod control is the key technical novelty relative to a conventional PWR and drives both the good load-following claim and the fuel/gadolinia qualification burden - it is a genuine first-of-a-kind element. GDA Step 3 completion by Dec 2026 is expected but not yet delivered, and DAC/SoDA are prerequisites for anything else. Coolant inlet/outlet temperatures and primary pressure are redacted in the public E3S case; steam conditions here are derived from the disclosed secondary-circuit range of 6-7 MPa. FID around 2029 means at least three more years of spend before any construction commitment. Cost estimate of GBP 2-3bn per unit (2024) implies roughly GBP 4,000-6,000/kW, which is credible only if the module factory learning curve materialises across a fleet that does not yet exist.

reactors.ramp_n: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024, Rolls-Royce SMR entry: 'The Rolls-Royce SMR is designed for full compliance with the U.K. Grid Code, provides load following between 50% and 100% power at a rate of 3-5% per minute'. Vendor states %/min directly, so no conversion. I record the top of the stated range; the bottom of the range (3 %Pr/min) already meets EUR KP14. Same source adds it 'can deliver stable operation for at least two hours supplying only the power station's house load'.
reactors.minload_n: 50 %Pr, from the same statement ('load following between 50% and 100% power'). This is reactor power reduction under UK Grid Code compliance, not steam bypass. Rolls-Royce also states frequency-sensitive-mode capability (E3S Case Chapter 1, section 1.5.3.1).
reactors.auto_n: Design requirements are published in the GDA E3S Case. Chapter 6 (Engineered Safety Features): 'safety measures shall be conservatively designed to deliver their functions without reliance on essential services supplied from on-site mobile equipment for 72 hours or from off-site for 7 days' (JN01-R-1435, JN02-R-2004). Important caveat: operator action IS credited relatively early - 'Class 1 and Class 2 safety measures shall be conservatively designed to deliver their functions without reliance on operator action in the MCR within 30 minutes, or outside of the MCR within 1 hour' (JN01-R-1636). Ultimate heat sink tank inventory: 24 h on one train, 72 h on two of three trains, at least 120 h on three of three. IAEA catalogue entry says passive heat removal is assured 'at least 72 hours, minimising the demand on human actions and electrical power.' So 72 h/7 d are autonomy-from-external-support figures; a strict 'no operator action at all' grace period of 72 h is NOT claimed.
reactors.avail_n: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024, Rolls-Royce SMR entry: 'An 18-day outage period is targeted to support high availability, at least 92.5% availability over the 60-year life of the Rolls-Royce SMR.' Two other vendor figures exist and differ: E3S Case Chapter 1 says 'at least 90% availability over the 60-year life', and the GDA technology page lists 'Expected capacity factor (%) >95'. I have taken the IAEA-catalogue figure of 92.5% as the middle, most specific claim and flag the spread.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments, and no announced EUR assessment found. The E3S Case Chapter 1 lists 'European Utility Requirements (EURs)' only as one of several relevant-good-practice sources informing design principles (section 1.1.2) - that is a design input, not an EUR assessment. UK ONR GDA Step 2 completion is a separate regulatory process.

reactors.name: SEALER-55
reactors.fuel: Uranium nitride (UN) pellets in alumina-forming corrosion-resistant steel cladding
reactors.fnote: Classified HALEU by the NucNet database; published SEALER-55 design work uses roughly 12% U-235 in UN fuel, but Blykalla has not confirmed a core-average figure publicly - treat 12% as indicative only. Uranium nitride fuel has no commercial fabrication line anywhere in the West and would require N-15 enrichment considerations plus a full qualification campaign; combined with no European HALEU enrichment at scale (Urenco's expansion not fully operational until ~2030), this is the least mature fuel route in the set. Vendor claims 25-year in-core fuel residence and '40% longer life' from UN's higher uranium density (vendor claim).
reactors.tnote: Compact primary system - vendor cites a roughly 5 x 5 m reactor unit and states the design 'avoids ultra heavy forging', which shortens production time and cost (vendor claim). Site footprint and module masses not published.

lic.j: Sweden (Government / Land and Environmental Court / SSM / Gavle municipality)
lic.s: Application submitted 19 May 2026 to build a six-unit, 330 MW SEALER reactor park at Norrsundet, Gavle municipality - Sweden's first-ever commercial application for an advanced reactor park. Triggers parallel government, environmental court, SSM and municipal reviews.

reactors.cnote: No nuclear construction. Blykalla broke ground in February 2025 on a non-nuclear Advanced Reactor Testing Site at Oskarshamn (with Uniper, KSB and ABB) for lead-loop, pump and component validation. A reactor factory is notionally targeted for construction from 2027.
reactors.codnote: Vendor and NucNet reporting point to first-half-2030s operation for the Norrsundet park, subject to permits and FID; earlier database entries showed a 2029-2030 target that has slipped. Vendor separately talks of commercial serial production in the 'early 2030s' (vendor claim).

orders.n: The six-unit Norrsundet park is Blykalla's own permit application, not a customer order; no FID. Sweden's state financing programme for new nuclear is the intended funding route. Data-centre and hyperscaler investors (KDDI, CoreWeave co-founders) are shareholders rather than offtakers.

reactors.health: Small but improving and well-connected. Raised $50M in December 2025 led by Oklo, Norrsken Launcher and Armada Investment, with KDDI, CoreWeave co-founders Brian Venturo and Peter Salanki, August One, GK Goh, Pitango, Nucleation Capital and Earth Venture Capital participating. Signed a Joint Technology Development Agreement with Oklo covering licensing, components, fuel sourcing and supply-chain alignment - notable strategic validation. Capital base is still an order of magnitude smaller than TerraPower/Oklo and the design is pre-licensing.
reactors.risks: Uranium nitride fuel is unproven commercially and has no Western fabrication supply chain - the single largest technical risk. Lead coolant corrosion of structural steels is the classic LFR failure mode; Blykalla's alumina-forming steels are its core IP but have limited long-duration irradiation data. Low 432C outlet temperature caps cycle efficiency and process-heat value relative to other LFRs. Swedish multi-agency permitting is untested for advanced reactors and the application was only filed in May 2026. No FID, no customer, no construction, thin capitalisation relative to a six-unit park.

reactors.name: SMR-300
reactors.fuel: UO2 in Framatome GAIA 17x17 assemblies, 69 assemblies, 29 RCCAs, soluble boron plus rod control
reactors.fnote: Core uses the Framatome GAIA 17x17 assembly already operating in US PWRs, enriched below 5% U-235 per Holtec's NRC core design update (Aug 2024). Commercially available fuel with an existing qualified supplier; only the active-length/loading pattern variant needs qualification. Lowest fuel risk after BWRX-300.
reactors.tnote: Holtec markets the SMR-300 as shippable by rail, barge or heavy road haul with factory-fabricated large components from its Camden NJ and Pittsburgh facilities (vendor claim). Heaviest single lift is not publicly disclosed. The lead site (Palisades) is on Lake Michigan, so barge access is available and the transport constraint is not being tested at the lead plant.

lic.s: Part 1 of a phased construction permit application (Pioneer Units 1 and 2) with limited work authorization and three exemption requests submitted 31 Dec 2025; accepted/docketed Feb 2026; environmental review scoping opened Jun 2026 (Docket ID NRC-2026-0265); Part 2 due no later than mid-2027
Pre-application engagement, topical/white paper reviews including core design update
GDA statement issued on completion of the two-step GDA; regulators found no fundamental shortfalls

reactors.cnote: Early site preparation is under way at Palisades (Covert, Michigan) under existing approved permits, ahead of the requested limited work authorization; no nuclear-safety-related concrete. Holtec/Hyundai have begun preparatory site construction planning for Pioneer 1 and 2. Holtec's claimed 'shovel-to-start' cycle of 2.5 years is unvalidated (vendor claim).
reactors.codnote: Holtec targets commissioning of both Pioneer units in the early 2030s under its 'Mission 2030' branding; the company expects them to be among the first SMRs commissioned in the US. Given Part 2 of the construction permit application is not due until mid-2027, 2032 is the earliest credible date and the vendor's 2030 branding is aspirational (vendor claim).

orders.n: Holtec is its own customer. Selected Dec 2025 for a USD 400 million DOE matching grant that becomes effective only after a funding agreement is negotiated and executed. Combined ~680 MWe alongside the restarted 800+ MWe Palisades PWR. No independent FID.
GDA completed Mar 2026 with Cottam as reference site; not selected in the Great British Energy - Nuclear SMR competition, which went to Rolls-Royce SMR.
Joint deployment proposal only, no contract.

reactors.health: Privately held, so limited public disclosure. Holtec is cash-generative from its dominant spent-fuel dry-storage and decommissioning businesses and is executing the Palisades restart (backed by a DOE loan guarantee facility and state support), which gives it operating revenue and nuclear-operator status that most SMR developers lack. Selected Dec 2025 for a USD 400m DOE matching grant, though this is conditional on executing a funding agreement. No bankruptcy, distress or layoff signals identified. Key structural weakness is that the SMR programme is self-funded and self-hosted rather than pulled by external paying customers, and there is no public audited balance sheet to verify capacity to carry a multi-billion-dollar FOAK build.
reactors.risks: Only Part 1 (limited work authorization plus environmental report) of the construction permit application is filed; the safety case in Part 2 is not due until mid-2027, so the design is much earlier in US regulatory review than the UK GDA completion implies. Key thermal-hydraulic parameters (RCS pressure, hot/cold leg temperatures, steam generator secondary conditions, cycle length) are redacted in all public NRC and GDA submissions - steam_temp_c, steam_pressure_bar and coolant_outlet_c here are engineering estimates from the disclosed Tavg of 578 F (303 C), 2250 psia RCS pressure and 1050 MWth, not regulator-confirmed values. Reported output is inconsistent: Holtec's GDA submission states a minimum 300 MWe net from 1050 MWth (28.6% net efficiency, unusually low), while the Palisades Pioneer units are described in NRC filings as 340 MWe each; an uprate or a definitional difference is unresolved. Holtec itself states load following 'is inherently wasteful' and does not recommend it, so the good load-following rating is capability, not intended duty. The no-EPZ claim is vendor-asserted and has not been adjudicated by the NRC. Single-customer, single-site concentration: if Palisades slips, the programme has no second anchor.

reactors.ramp_n: No ramp rate published by Holtec or any regulator. Holtec technical bulletin HTB-085 Rev 5 says only 'SMR-300 can be configured to load follow which is inherently wasteful of energy' - which implies steam bypass rather than reactor power reduction, but Holtec gives no rate and no units. Nothing in the IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 SMR-300 entry either.
reactors.minload_n: Not published. Holtec's phrase 'load follow which is inherently wasteful of energy' suggests plant-side (steam dump) flexibility rather than reactor power reduction, so the reactor would not follow load; but Holtec does not state a minimum stable reactor power, so this is inference and I am not assigning a number.
reactors.auto_n: Only unquantified claims found. Holtec HTB-085 Rev 5: 'limitless coping period after a postulated hypothetical loss-of-coolant accident' and 'The plant does not need operator intervention in the wake of any accident'. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 SMR-300 entry: passive systems 'designed to function without operator intervention'. These are vendor marketing phrases with no hour or day figure attached, and no NRC-confirmed grace or coping time was found (SMR-300 is in NRC pre-application). Not converted into numbers.
reactors.avail_n: No percentage published. Holtec claims 'High-capacity factor through very short refueling outages' and 'the refueling of the plant is estimated to take no more than 7 calendar days', but states no availability or capacity factor number.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments. No announced EUR assessment found.

reactors.name: SSR-W300 (Stable Salt Reactor - Wasteburner)
reactors.vendor: Moltex Energy Canada Inc. (parent Moltex Energy Ltd, UK - in administration)
reactors.coolant: ZrF4-KF fluoride coolant salt (stabilised with ZrF2) in an unpressurised pool; molten nitrate salt secondary/GridReserve loop. Fuel salt is static inside vented fuel tubes, not pumped.
reactors.fuel: Molten chloride fuel salt held statically in vertical vented fuel tubes assembled into conventional-looking assemblies; approx. 25% reactor-grade PuCl3 / 30% UCl3 / 45% KCl. Fast spectrum.
reactors.fnote: Weakest fuel supply position of the six. The SSR-W does not use enriched uranium at all - it runs on reactor-grade plutonium and uranium chlorides recovered from CANDU used fuel via Moltex's WATSS (Waste To Stable Salt) process, so it is classed HALEU-equivalent here purely on fissile content and safeguards category, not on enrichment. WATSS was only bench-validated by Moltex Energy Canada in March 2025 (claimed 90% transuranic extraction in a ~24-hour chemical process, vendor claim); there is no licensed WATSS plant, no Canadian policy decision permitting separation of plutonium from CANDU used fuel, and no alternative fuel source - the reactor cannot start without it. Li-7 exposure: NONE. Chloride fuel salt and ZrF4-KF coolant contain no lithium, so the SSR-W is entirely insulated from the Russian/Chinese Li-7 monopoly that constrains Saltfoss, Copenhagen Atomics and TMSR-LF1. The analogous isotopic question for chloride fast reactors is Cl-37 enrichment (to suppress Cl-35(n,p)S-35 corrosion products and long-lived Cl-36 waste); Moltex has argued its design tolerates natural chlorine, but this is a vendor claim and no commercial Cl-37 enrichment industry exists either.
reactors.tnote: Fuel assemblies are truck-transportable and handled with broadly conventional fuel-handling equipment (a key claimed simplification). The reactor tank/pool itself is a large site-fabricated or heavy-lift component. No published module transport weights (vendor claim on assembly handling; tank transport class inferred, not verified).

lic.s: Vendor Design Review Phase 1 completed; CNSC flagged inadequate quality assurance programmes and absence of a secondary control room. No Phase 2 completion, no site preparation licence applied for, no licence application.

reactors.cnote: No construction, no site preparation licence application. The intended host site was NB Power's Point Lepreau. In October 2025 New Brunswick Energy Minister Rene Legacy stated the province would no longer wait for the domestic SMR developers; on 30 March 2026 the NB Power review panel effectively rejected FOAK SMRs, with panel member Duncan Hawthorne stating 'We don't think it's appropriate for NB Power to be playing in a first-of-a-kind world', and instead recommended considering an additional large-scale proven-technology nuclear plant alongside Point Lepreau. The project has lost its host utility.
reactors.codnote: No credible COD. Prior guidance was for a Point Lepreau demonstration unit in the early 2030s; with the UK parent in administration since April 2025, no completed sale as of 7 August 2026, and New Brunswick formally stepping away, no date can be supported.

orders.c: NB Power / Province of New Brunswick
orders.n: Development support only, never an order or FID. CEDAR (March 2026) totals CAD 60.67M in public support: CAD 6.5M New Brunswick, CAD 1M Ontario Power Generation, CAD 53.17M federal. No private-sector investment ever materialised. Province publicly disengaged October 2025.

reactors.health: Distressed - the worst of the six. UK parent Moltex Energy Limited was placed into administration on/around 2 April 2025 with Azets appointed administrators, after directors could not obtain majority shareholder consent for new investment or an asset sale; assets (IP, subsidiary shareholdings, WATSS, SSR-W, MoltexFLEX) have been marketed for sale, including via Hilco. The CBC reported the insolvency risk in April 2025; in July 2025 the former CEO sued for wrongful dismissal, disclosing staffing had been cut by more than a quarter around two years earlier and that shareholders had blocked the Canadian subsidiary's fundraising. As of 7 August 2026 the sale is still not closed: preferred purchaser Nuclea Energy Inc. (Ontario) abandoned its planned USD 50M NYSE IPO and instead pursued a reverse merger with Nasdaq-listed Mangoceuticals Inc. (a Dallas telemedicine company) to reach public markets faster, with its announcements focused on its own 'Morpheus Micro Reactor' rather than Moltex. Moltex CEO Rory O'Sullivan says 'We are still in exclusive negotiations with Nuclea' and the administrator confirms negotiations remain ongoing, but neither party's official announcements mention Moltex going forward. Treat as effectively non-viable pending a funded buyer.
reactors.risks: Corporate insolvency is the dominant risk - parent in administration 16+ months with no closed sale and a prospective buyer whose own financing has failed and pivoted. Host utility and province have withdrawn. Fuel supply is existential: no WATSS plant, no policy authorisation to separate plutonium from CANDU used fuel, and no substitute fuel. CNSC has only completed Phase 1 VDR, with QA and secondary-control-room deficiencies noted. Vented fuel tube integrity, chloride salt corrosion and Cl-36/S-35 waste behaviour are unresolved technically. Offsetting positives - genuine 8-hour GridReserve nitrate thermal storage giving excellent load following, and complete freedom from the Li-7 supply chain - are real but unbankable in the current corporate state.

reactors.ramp_n: No number published, and Moltex explicitly declines to give one from the nuclear side. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 SSR-W entry: 'The ramp rates of the plant will be driven by the steam side, not the nuclear side.' That locates the limit in the balance of plant but supplies no %/min or MW/min figure, so no conversion is possible.
reactors.minload_n: Not published, and the flexibility mechanism is a THERMAL STORE rather than reactor power reduction. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 SSR-W entry rates the plant as '750 / 300 continuous as baseload, 750 / 900 as 8-hour peaking plant' - i.e. 300 MWe baseload with the GridReserve molten-salt store enabling 900 MWe for 8 hours at constant 750 MWt reactor power. The plant follows load; the reactor does not. No minimum plant output is stated.
reactors.auto_n: Only an unquantified claim. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 SSR-W entry states the design can 'take decay heat away indefinitely in an accident scenario'. 'Indefinitely' is a vendor phrase with no supporting duration published, so I have not converted it into a number. CNSC Vendor Design Review is under way; no CNSC-confirmed figure found.
reactors.avail_n: No availability or capacity factor percentage published.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Out of EUR SMLWR scope (molten salt fast reactor).

reactors.name: ThorCon 500 (TMSR-500)
reactors.fuel: Liquid fluoride fuel salt in a sealed replaceable 'Can'; hybrid thorium/uranium, LEU driver blended with thorium
reactors.fnote: Split verdict. Li-7 exposure: NONE by design - the fuel and coolant salts are sodium-beryllium fluoride (NaF-BeF2), and World Nuclear Association explicitly notes 'Li-7 fluoride is avoided for cost reasons'. This is the single smartest supply-chain decision in the ThorCon design and removes the Russian/Chinese enriched-lithium dependency entirely. The trade-off is beryllium: BeF2 at 12 mol% across a 1,114 MWth two-module plant implies a large beryllium inventory, and BeF2 is acutely toxic (chronic beryllium disease), tightly regulated, and supplied by a very small number of producers globally - a different but real chokepoint. The harder problem is uranium: IAEA ARIS gives enrichment as ~5.0% average / 19.7% maximum, i.e. the driver uranium is HALEU at just under 20%. Commercial HALEU supply outside Russia is minimal (Centrus is producing only at demonstration scale under DOE contract), and Indonesia has no domestic enrichment and no established HALEU supply agreement. A HALEU-dependent FOAK in a newcomer nuclear state with no fuel contract is a first-order schedule risk. Thorium feedstock itself is abundant and cheap (Indonesia has monazite from tin tailings on Bangka) and is not a constraint. There is no commercial fluoride fuel-salt fabricator anywhere for a plant of this size.
reactors.tnote: IAEA ARIS gives the Can as 10.3 m long x 7.8 m diameter at 343,000 kg transport weight (dry, without salt). ThorCon's core commercial premise is shipyard block construction: the entire plant is built in a shipyard on a hull/barge, floated to the moored site and ballasted down, with Cans disconnected and shipped back to a central service facility after their 8-year life. This mandates a coastal or near-shore site (Kelasa Island, Bangka Belitung) and rules out inland siting.

lic.s: Pre-licensing consultation opened

Application submitted for site evaluation - Site Evaluation Programme (PET) and Site Evaluation Management System (SMET) documents filed by PT ThorCon Power Indonesia; first NPP licence applicant in Indonesian history

Site evaluation programme and management system APPROVED - Decree No. 00003.556.1.300725. This authorises the site survey/evaluation campaign only. Still required per BAPETEN Regulation No. 1/2022: Site Permit, Design Approval, Construction Permit, Commissioning Approval, Operating Licence.

reactors.cnote: No construction. Regulatory status is site-evaluation-approved only - four further BAPETEN permits stand between the project and operation. Bureau Veritas engaged to support development. Indonesia's 2025-2034 RUPTL electricity supply plan includes nuclear, which improves the policy backdrop, but no construction permit exists and no shipyard slot has been announced.
reactors.codnote: Company targets Indonesia's first operational NPP 'by 2032 or earlier' (vendor claim). Given that only the site evaluation programme has been approved as of mid-2025, that four major permits remain, that no HALEU supply is contracted and no financing is closed, 2032 should be treated as aspirational; late 2030s is more realistic.

orders.n: No purchase order and no FID. PT ThorCon Power Indonesia submitted a proposal to the National Energy Council (DEN) and the project appears in the 2025-2034 RUPTL context, but this is policy inclusion rather than procurement. Earlier reporting put the required capital at roughly Rp 17 trillion with no disclosed committed financing.

reactors.health: Small, privately held and thinly capitalised relative to the task - a two-unit 500 MWe FOAK. Notably, the project drew explicit political scepticism in Indonesia even after the July 2025 site approval: House Commission XII Chairman Bambang Patijaya publicly questioned the company's standing, noting that the US Embassy did not recognise it as a developer or operator of nuclear power plants, and Indonesian officials have signalled a preference for proven PWR technology with an operating track record. Financing for the plant has not been demonstrated. The company has no completed reactor anywhere and no revenue.
reactors.risks: HALEU supply is uncontracted and structurally scarce outside Russia. Beryllium fluoride toxicity, handling and supply concentration replace the Li-7 problem rather than eliminating supply risk. Political and institutional credibility challenged in the Indonesian legislature, with a stated preference for PWRs. Financing unproven. Newcomer-country regulator (BAPETEN) has never licensed a power reactor, let alone a liquid-fuelled Gen IV one, so the regulatory schedule is unpredictable in both directions. Barge-mounted moored siting off Bangka carries marine, seismic and security exposure. Offsetting strengths: real ARIS-documented design maturity, supercritical steam at 547 C / 255 bar giving high efficiency, a 0.5 km EPZ claim, and the only genuinely Li-7-free fluoride design in this set.

reactors.ramp_n: No rate published. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 Thorcon entry describes the mechanism only: 'Load following relies on reactor physics. As electric power demand decreases, less heat is removed' from the salt, and the negative temperature coefficient reduces power. No %/min or MW/min figure is given, so no conversion is possible.
reactors.minload_n: Not published. The claimed mechanism is inherent reactivity feedback in the fuel salt (reactor power genuinely follows load), not a thermal store or steam bypass - but Thorcon states no minimum stable power level.
reactors.auto_n: Mixed quantified and unquantified claims; I have recorded only the quantified one. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 Thorcon entry: 'No operator intervention is needed at any time. No electric power is necessary, though fans keep basement' cool; the passive cooling water inventory provides 'cooling for at least 40 days. Cooling time can be extended indefinitely by supplying more water from' external sources; and 'Cooling using natural air flow continues indefinitely.' I record coping_d = 40 (a floor, 'at least') because it is a stated inventory-based figure, and leave grace_h null because 'no operator intervention is needed at any time' is an unbounded claim with no analysed duration behind it. The 'indefinitely' extension explicitly depends on external water supply, so it is not a no-external-resources figure.
reactors.avail_n: No availability or capacity factor percentage published in the IAEA entry or reachable ThorCon material.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Out of EUR SMLWR scope on two counts: molten salt reactor, and the reference plant is a shipyard-built floating/barge-mounted power plant, which the Key Positions explicitly exclude.

reactors.name: TMSR-LF1 (Thorium Molten Salt Reactor - Liquid Fuel 1), Wuwei
reactors.vendor: Shanghai Institute of Applied Physics (SINAP), Chinese Academy of Sciences
reactors.coolant: FLiBe (LiF-BeF2) fuel salt with 99.95% enriched Li-7, containing UF4 and ThF4; graphite-moderated, thermal spectrum. Research reactor - no power conversion system.
reactors.fuel: Liquid fluoride fuel salt - UF4 dissolved in FLiBe with a thorium (ThF4) inventory of approximately 50 kg and a FLiBe fertile blanket at 99.95% Li-7
reactors.fnote: The only entity on earth that has actually manufactured, loaded and operated a lithium-7 fluoride MSR fuel salt at scale - which makes it the reference point for judging everyone else's claims, and the reason China is the benchmark. The core salt is FLiBe with 99.95% Li-7, and SINAP has separately developed a centrifugal-extraction route reported to reach 99.99% Li-7 purity, giving China a domestic Li-7 capability independent of Russia (though World Nuclear Association notes China has also been buying Russian Li-7 from TVEL's Novosibirsk plant, which supplies up to 80% of world demand). Uranium is enriched to under 20% (HALEU), domestically supplied. The programme reports over 90% localisation with core equipment entirely domestically sourced, backed by a roughly USD 3.3bn national programme and nearly 100 participating institutes, universities and industrial groups. Rated 4 rather than 5 because none of this supply chain is exportable or available to non-Chinese projects, and 2 MWth is not yet proof of tonne-scale commercial fuel-salt manufacture. For Western screening purposes the correct read is: the Li-7 bottleneck is solvable - China solved it - but solving it took a state programme of that size and roughly two decades, which is the realistic yardstick for Saltfoss, Copenhagen Atomics or any FLiBe design outside China.
reactors.tnote: Site-built research facility, not a transportable product. Sited at Wuwei in the Gobi desert region of Gansu Province specifically because a molten salt reactor needs no large water heat sink - the strongest real-world demonstration in this set that MSRs enable arid-site deployment.

lic.s: Operating permit issued for the experimental reactor
First criticality achieved 11 October 2023; full-power operation June 2024; online refuelling demonstrated without shutdown; thorium loaded October 2024

reactors.cnote: OPERATING - the world's only operating liquid-fuel molten salt reactor and the reference case for this entire technology class. Construction began September 2018, completed August 2021 (ahead of the original 2024 schedule), operating licence June 2023, first criticality 11 October 2023, full-power operation June 2024, thorium added October 2024, and on 1 November 2025 SINAP announced the first thorium-uranium fuel conversion ever achieved in a molten salt reactor - the first international experimental data of its kind. Conversion ratio approximately 0.1 with roughly 50 kg thorium inventory. Refuelling has been demonstrated without shutting the reactor down, validating the central operational claim of the liquid-fuel MSR concept.
reactors.codnote: Not a commercial plant - no electrical output and no COD in the commercial sense. First criticality 11 October 2023 and full-power operation June 2024 are the operational milestones. Follow-on programme: a 10 MW demonstration reactor targeted by 2029 and 100 MWth-class demonstration/power stations targeted by 2035 (state programme targets; the 10 MW and 100 MW figures are reported inconsistently as MWe vs MWth across sources and should be verified before use).

orders.c: Chinese Academy of Sciences / Chinese state programme
orders.n: Built and funded as a national R&D programme (~USD 3.3bn), not a commercial sale. FID marked true because the reactor was funded, built and is operating. No export offering and no commercial orders exist.

reactors.health: Strongest of the six by a wide margin, but not a vendor in the commercial sense. SINAP is an institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, executing a state-funded programme reported at roughly USD 3.3bn with nearly 100 participating Chinese institutes, universities and industrial groups and over 90% equipment localisation. No commercial, financing or insolvency risk. The relevant limitation for a Western screening database is availability: this technology is not for sale or export, so it functions as a technical benchmark and a source of validated operating data rather than a procurable option.
reactors.risks: Not procurable - no export offering, so its value to a screening exercise is as a reference datum, not a candidate. Scale gap is enormous: 2 MWth with no power conversion versus 250-750 MWth commercial concepts, so materials lifetime data (Hastelloy N corrosion, graphite dimensional change under fluence, tritium management) at commercial power density and duration remains unproven. Conversion ratio of ~0.1 is far from breakeven breeding, so the thorium fuel cycle is demonstrated in principle but nowhere near closed. Published operating data is limited and filtered through state announcements, so independent verification of availability, corrosion rates and salt chemistry performance is not possible. The 2029 and 2035 follow-on dates are state targets with no independent schedule verification.

reactors.ramp_n: No rate published, and the attribute is largely inapplicable. TMSR-LF1 is a 2 MWt liquid-fuel thorium molten salt EXPERIMENTAL reactor at Wuwei, Gansu, operated by SINAP/Chinese Academy of Sciences. It has no electrical generating plant, so a %Pr/min electrical ramp does not exist. No SINAP or NNSA statement on load following was found, and TMSR-LF1 does not appear in the IAEA ARIS SMR Catalogue 2024.
reactors.minload_n: Not published; not meaningful for a 2 MWt research reactor with no power conversion system.
reactors.auto_n: No grace period or coping time published. Public reporting (CAS, World Nuclear News, POWER) covers the operating permit, sustained operation and the 2025 thorium-uranium conversion milestone, but contains no safety-function autonomy durations. China's NNSA licensed the reactor but I found no published NNSA grace or coping figure. Nothing to record.
reactors.avail_n: No availability or capacity factor figure published. As an experimental reactor run on a research campaign basis, a design availability figure would not normally be quoted.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. Out of EUR SMLWR scope (molten salt experimental reactor).
