reactors.name: VOYGR / NuScale Power Module US460 (77 MWe module)
reactors.fuel: UO2, 17x17 array with ~2 m active length (approximately half-height PWR assembly), 37 assemblies per module
reactors.fnote: LEU below 5% so no HALEU dependency, but the assembly is a non-standard shortened 17x17 design (NuFuel-HTP2 lineage, Framatome) that no vendor currently fabricates commercially. A dedicated production line must be qualified and licensed before first core. NuScale reports 60+ supply-chain partners and 30+ executed agreements but no fuel line is in serial production (vendor claim).
reactors.tnote: NPM is ~23 m tall x ~4.6 m diameter and ~700 t fully assembled; shipped in three major sections by barge, rail or specialised heavy haul and assembled on site. Vendor states rail/truck/barge are all feasible (vendor claim); in practice barge or rail is the realistic route for the largest sections.

lic.s: Standard Design Approval issued for US460 (6x77 MWe); final safety evaluation report 28 May 2025, SDA 29 May 2025, Federal Register notice 4 Jun 2025
Prior US600 (50 MWe module) standard design certification rulemaking completed 2023; superseded commercially by US460
Doicesti project licensing in progress post-FID; site-specific permitting and pre-EPC phase (~15 months) underway

reactors.cnote: No nuclear construction anywhere. At Doicesti, Romania, the former 600 MW coal plant has been fully demolished (600,000 t removed) with a 650 MW grid connection retained, and geotechnical work plus pre-EPC contracting is underway - genuine site preparation but not first concrete. The earlier UAMPS/Carbon Free Power Project in Idaho was cancelled in Nov 2023, so this design has already lost one first-of-a-kind host.
reactors.codnote: RoPower/Doicesti targeted for 'the beginning of the next decade' (~2030-2031), explicitly subject to approvals (developer claim). The TVA/ENTRA1 6 GW programme has no announced COD and no executed PPA.

orders.n: FID approved by Nuclearelectrica shareholders 12 Feb 2026 for a VOYGR-6 (462 MWe gross) at Doicesti. FID is conditional on a set of mandatory conditions held under an eight-year confidentiality agreement - if any single condition is unmet the project is deemed unfeasible. Treat as a qualified FID, not an unconditional one.

orders.c: Tennessee Valley Authority via ENTRA1 Energy
orders.n: Sep 2025 collaborative agreement for up to 6 GW of NuScale SMR deployment, described as the largest US nuclear deployment programme in history. As of Q2 2026 this is still a collaborative agreement only - no definitive PPA has been executed and no site or unit count is contractually fixed.

reactors.health: Weakest revenue position but strong balance sheet. NuScale Power (NYSE: SMR) reported Q2 2026 revenue of roughly USD 0.1 million (down ~99% year on year, an ~USD 8.0m decline versus Q2 2025 following completion of the Fluor RoPower FEED-2 work) and continues to run material net losses, but ended the quarter with ~USD 1.9 billion in cash, equivalents and investments. No bankruptcy or going-concern risk in the near term; the real issue is a near-zero revenue base and a commercial model in which ENTRA1 Energy holds exclusive global commercialisation rights, which analysts have flagged as raising funding and disclosure questions. NuScale already absorbed the 2023 cancellation of the UAMPS/CFPP project and associated restructuring.
reactors.risks: Only US design in this set with a regulator-issued standard design approval, but zero units under construction and no unconditional order. Twelve modules of NPM hardware were long-lead-fabricated for the cancelled CFPP and their reusability for the uprated US460 is not confirmed. Shortened non-standard fuel assembly requires a new qualified fabrication line - the single largest schedule risk. Very low per-module output (77 MWe) means high unit count, high total N-th-of-a-kind module count and heavy dependence on serial factory learning that has never been demonstrated. Economics were the stated reason for the CFPP cancellation and have not been independently re-validated. Site-boundary EPZ rests on an NRC-accepted methodology (ACRS validated 2022) and is design-approved but has not been applied at a licensed operating site. Air-cooling and dry-cooling capability is vendor-stated. Commercial dependence on a single intermediary (ENTRA1) concentrates counterparty risk. 500 C / 69 bar process steam is achievable only with external compression and supplementary heating (about 86% of the enthalpy from nuclear heat) - direct nuclear steam is 283 C at 32.8 bar (vendor claim). AUDIT: no primary source confirms physical site works at Doicesti following the February 2026 RoPower FID.

reactors.ramp_n: Derived from NuScale's own published manoeuvre times (WP-178373 Rev 1, Table 4). Turbine bypass: 20%->100% in 27 min => 80/27 = 2.96 %Pr/min up; 100%->20% in 8 min => 80/8 = 10 %Pr/min down. Control rods only (reactor power): 20%->100% in 96 min => 80/96 = 0.83 %Pr/min up; 100%->20% in <24 min => >3.33 %Pr/min down. The binding sustained up-ramp of electrical output is therefore ~2.96 %Pr/min and depends on 100% turbine bypass capability. Separately, EPRI URD Rev 13 required NuScale to achieve 40%/hour = 0.67 %Pr/min (ANL/NuScale ICAPP-15 paper).
reactors.minload_n: 20 %Pr, stated by NuScale for a single module. Achievable two ways: reactor power reduction by control rods (NuScale states rod-only manoeuvres down to 40% reactor power without boron adjustment) or by dumping steam through the 100% turbine bypass to the condenser. In bypass mode the plant follows load while the reactor stays at power - the flexibility is thermal, not nuclear. Below ~40% reactor power, boron adjustment is involved.
reactors.auto_n: NuScale and IAEA state an 'unlimited' claim, which I have not converted into an unbounded number. IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024, NuScale entry, Distinguishing features: 'Unlimited time for core cooling without AC or DC power, water addition, or operator action'; text: 'There are no design basis accidents that uncover the core or require operator action.' The concrete analysed bound published by NuScale authors (Frontiers in Energy Research 2023) is: 'the pool absorbs all decay heat produced by all reactors for more than 30 days'; 'After 30 days, water boil-off and passive air cooling of the modules provide adequate cooling for an unlimited period of time'; 'Water boil-off will uncover the DHRS condenser by 30 days and the pool will be effectively empty by 99 days'. I therefore record 30 days (720 h) as the quantified, analysis-backed figure and flag the 'unlimited' phrasing as the vendor's own.
reactors.avail_n: IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 NuScale entry: 'The nominal plant capacity factor is 95% with a refuelling outage time of 10 days'. NuScale white paper WP-178373: 'The expected capacity factor of a NuScale-based SMR power plant is >= 95%, which assumes a well-defined 10-day refueling outage for an 18-month fuel cycle and a conservatively assumed 3% forced outages.' Vendor-stated, not regulator-confirmed.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments (13 large LWRs). No announced EUR assessment found. US NRC Standard Design Approval for US460 is a different process and is not an EUR assessment.

reactors.name: Xe-100
reactors.fuel: TRISO-X UCO TRISO particles in 6 cm graphite pebbles; ~220,000 pebbles per core, ~160 GWd/tHM target burnup
reactors.fnote: TRISO-X received the first-ever NRC 10 CFR Part 70 Category II license for commercial HALEU fuel fabrication on 13 Feb 2026; TX-1 plant at Oak Ridge Horizon Center still under vertical construction, completion guided to 1H2028. Nameplate ~5 tU/yr = ~700,000 pebbles/yr, enough for as many as 11 Xe-100 reactors (vendor claim). Initial Dow/Long Mott core HALEU allocated from DOE HALEU Availability Program; a definitive LEU+HALEU enrichment-services agreement with Centrus was signed 6 Aug 2026 but quantities and delivery dates are undisclosed and only cover 'a portion' of the 11.5 GW pipeline. Net: fuel is the schedule-critical path — licensed but not yet producing.
reactors.tnote: Reactor pressure vessel and steam generator pressure vessel are among the largest safety-critical steel components; under the 18 Dec 2025 binding reservation agreement Doosan Enerbility will fabricate them at Changwon, South Korea (new SMR factory, ~20 Xe-100 vessel sets/yr at full rate), implying ocean/heavy-lift then barge or heavy-haul delivery. No published module weights; Long Mott (Seadrift) and Cascade (Richland, Columbia River) are both barge-accessible sites.

lic.s: Construction permit application under review — Long Mott Generating Station, 4 modules, 800 MWth/320 MWe, Calhoun County TX. Submitted 31 Mar 2025, accepted 12 May 2025, draft safety evaluation sections Feb 2026, Environmental Assessment with FONSI issued 18 May 2026. Advanced SER target Aug 2026, final SER target Nov 2026; mandatory hearing and permit decision TBD.
TRISO-X TX-1 special nuclear material (Part 70) license issued for HALEU TRISO fuel fabrication; NRC readiness inspection still required before operations

reactors.cnote: No construction permit issued yet, so no nuclear construction. Fluor was awarded Front-End Loading Stage 2 (FEL-2) services for the Seadrift/Long Mott project on 6 Apr 2026 (project definition, feasibility, cost and risk). The Cascade project with Energy Northwest near Richland, WA is still pre-application (environmental reviews and permitting prep with AtkinsRéalis).
reactors.codnote: Dow/Long Mott targeted for 'early 2030s'; Dow's final funding decision is expected only after the operating licence application, potentially around 2028. Cascade: construction start 'by the end of this decade', operations 'in the 2030s'. Amazon/X-energy have stated a goal of >5 GW of Xe-100 projects online by 2039 (vendor claim). 2031 used here as a nominal first-unit COD; no firm vendor-committed COD exists.

orders.c: Dow (Long Mott Energy LLC, UCC Seadrift Operations)
orders.n: Construction permit application filed; DOE ARDP cost-shared. Three units for power, one supplying ~200 MWth as industrial steam. Dow FID not taken.

orders.c: Energy Northwest / Amazon (Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, Richland WA)
orders.n: Initial 4 modules (320 MWe), expandable to 12 modules (~960 MWe). Amazon Climate Pledge Fund capital plus rights to offtake; pre-application stage, no FID.

orders.c: Centrica (UK) and exploration agreements with Louisville Gas & Electric and Talen Energy
orders.n: Non-binding pipeline entries; X-energy reports a total pipeline of 144 reactors / ~11.5 GWe across US and UK (vendor claim).

reactors.health: Strong and improved sharply in 2026. Closed an oversubscribed $700M Series D (Nov 2025) after a $700M Series C-1 (Feb 2025), then IPO'd on Nasdaq (ticker XE) in April 2026 raising ~$1.02B gross / ~$1.1B net, with a ~31% first-day pop. Q1 2026: revenue and grant income $43.4M (+109% y/y), operating expenses $109.5M, total liquidity $944.0M as of 31 Mar 2026 before IPO proceeds. Amazon is a strategic investor; Doosan and DL E&C are strategic shareholders/suppliers. Burn rate is high and the company is deeply pre-revenue on reactor sales.
reactors.risks: No construction permit yet — first-of-a-kind NRC construction permit decision still pending after final SER (target Nov 2026) plus mandatory hearing. Dow FID is a separate and later gate (~2028), so the anchor order is not committed. TRISO-X TX-1 completion (1H2028) is on the critical path and HALEU enrichment supply beyond the DOE allocation is not quantified. 565 °C / 165 bar superheated steam is the most aggressive steam condition of any Western SMR and drives helical steam-generator and Alloy 800H/high-temperature materials risk plus helium-to-water boundary integrity concerns; the 750 °C helium outlet also pushes graphite and metallic internals qualification. Load-following claim (40%–100% in 12 minutes) is a vendor claim and unproven at plant scale. Air-cooling capability is thermodynamically plausible at these steam conditions but is NOT confirmed in the primary sources reviewed — treat as unverified. EPZ: X-energy's licensing white paper states it 'anticipates that the boundary of the EPZ for the Xe-100 coincides with the site area boundary', but no fixed distance has been approved, so epz_km is left null. Footprint and module weights are not published.

reactors.ramp_n: Derived from X-energy's own statement: the Xe-100 is 'designed to ramp up or ramp down between 40% and full power in 12 minutes'. Arithmetic: (100-40) %Pr / 12 min = 60/12 = 5.0 %Pr/min. Consistent with the IAEA ARIS Catalogue 2024 Xe-100 entry, which describes control-rod worth sized to 'allow for load-follow operation' over '100%-40%-100%'. This is reactor power reduction in a pebble-bed HTGR, not a thermal store. Meets EUR KP14's 3 %Pr/min - though note EUR KP on SMLWR does not apply to a gas-cooled design.
reactors.minload_n: 40 %Pr, stated by X-energy as the bottom of the load-follow band ('between 40% and full power') and corroborated by the IAEA entry's '100%-40%-100%' load-follow description. Reactor power reduction, not steam bypass.
reactors.auto_n: No hour or day figure published. X-energy relies on inherent characteristics: 'if temperatures rise, the nuclear reaction naturally slows and stops', TRISO functional containment, and passive core heat removal 'if the [active] removal system is not available, then the core heat is removed passively through: Conduction between...' (IAEA entry). Neither X-energy nor the NRC (pre-application / construction permit stage for the Long Mott project) publishes a quantified grace period or coping time that I could find. Not converted from qualitative claims.
reactors.avail_n: X-energy's Xe-100 product page lists '95%' as 'Target Reliability'. Note the label is reliability, not availability or capacity factor, so this is a soft match to EUR KP13. The IAEA entry adds only qualitative statements ('high plant availability', 'due to online refuelling features a better availability factor can be expected'). Vendor-stated.
reactors.eur_n: Not on the EUR Association's published list of completed Volume 3 design assessments; no announced EUR assessment found. In any case EUR Key Positions on SMLWR cover water-cooled designs only.

haleu.status: Commercially near-nonexistent outside Russia. As of mid-2026 the only Western commercial-scale HALEU enrichment in operation is Centrus Energy's American Centrifuge Plant at Piketon, Ohio, running a single 16-machine cascade at a nameplate rate of about 900 kg HALEU per year under a DOE demonstration contract that was extended for a further year in June 2025; Centrus reached the cumulative 900 kg delivered milestone in 2025. Rosatom's TVEL remains the only entity with genuine at-scale HALEU capability, and the US Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act closes that route. DOE is bridging near-term demand by downblending surplus HEU and has finalised three HALEU allocation contracts; the HALEU Availability Program made its first allocations to five advanced reactor developers in April 2025, added conditional commitments in August 2025, and has since allocated material for space and defence uses including NASA and Radiant.
suppliers: Centrus Energy / American Centrifuge Operating (Piketon, Ohio - only operating Western commercial HALEU enricher)
US DOE (downblended surplus HEU from Savannah River and Y-12, allocated via the HALEU Availability Program)
Urenco (Capenhurst UK HALEU facility, targeted 2031; Urenco USA Eunice producing LEU+ only)
Orano (LEU/LEU+ expansion; Project Ike at Oak Ridge is LEU not HALEU)
General Matter (Paducah, Kentucky - construction from 2026, operations targeted 2034)
Global Laser Enrichment (SILEX/GLE - development stage)
Rosatom/TVEL (only at-scale incumbent; blocked for US and most Western buyers)
haleu.capacity_note: Centrus ~900 kg/yr today from the existing cascade; its DOE-backed Piketon expansion, for which Fluor was named EPC contractor in February 2026 under a $900m task order awarded January 2026, targets roughly 6,000 kg/yr of HALEU from a new cascade. General Matter received a $900m task order for HALEU at Paducah with operations targeted 2034. Urenco's Capenhurst HALEU line, supported by about $245m/£196m of UK government funding with Costain on design, is specified at up to 27 tU HALEU per year from 2031. Urenco USA started up the first phase of its Eunice expansion in May 2025 reaching about 4,650 tSWU/y, targeting 5,000 tSWU/y in 2026-27 and announcing a further major expansion in 2026 toward roughly 7,100 tSWU/y - but this is LEU/LEU+, not HALEU. Aggregate confirmed Western HALEU capacity in 2026 is therefore on the order of one tonne per year, against advanced-reactor demand estimates in the tens of tonnes per year by the early 2030s.
haleu.bottleneck: A single-supplier, single-cascade Western production base with a five-to-eight year lead time to meaningful tonnage. Secondary bottlenecks: DOE-allocated downblended HEU is a finite bridge, not a supply chain; Urenco USA (LES), the only commercially operating enricher in the US, received no task order in the January 2026 DOE awards despite being selected in October 2024, so US capacity growth is concentrated in two less-proven entrants; and HALEU output is coupled to the transport-package and fabrication constraints below, so tonnage alone does not unlock fuel delivery.

triso.status: First commercial-scale Western line licensed but not yet producing. X-energy's TRISO-X TF3 facility at Oak Ridge, Tennessee received the first-ever NRC Category II licence for commercial advanced nuclear fuel fabrication on 13 February 2026, valid 40 years to 2066. Vertical construction started in November 2025 with core-and-shell completion expected mid-2026; the NRC must complete an operational readiness review before uranium can be introduced, so no commercial TRISO has been fabricated at TF3 as of mid-2026. BWXT operates the only currently producing Western TRISO line, at Lynchburg, Virginia, where it has commissioned new furnace capacity under DOE support and is evaluating a greenfield TRISO facility to meet demand.
suppliers: X-energy / TRISO-X (TF3, Oak Ridge, Tennessee - licensed February 2026, not yet operating)
BWX Technologies (Lynchburg, Virginia - only currently producing Western TRISO line)
Kairos Power (in-house pebble fabrication for Hermes, development scale)
Idaho National Laboratory and Oak Ridge National Laboratory (AGR programme, laboratory and qualification scale)
China National Nuclear Corporation (HTR-PM pebble line, not available to Western buyers)
triso.capacity_note: TF3 is designed for 25 MTU/yr at full build-out: line TX-1 at 5 MTU/yr (roughly 700,000 pebbles per year) with TX-2 in design to bring the combined total to 20 MTU/yr and the site to 25 MTU/yr. Construction is a $768m, roughly five-year programme with peak staffing of 332. BWXT's Lynchburg throughput is not publicly quantified in metric tonnes per year but is qualification and demonstration scale rather than fleet scale. Total Western commercial TRISO output in 2026 is effectively zero on a fleet basis.
triso.bottleneck: Sequencing. TF3 must pass operational readiness review and ramp TX-1 before any commercial deliveries, and TX-2 is still in design, so meaningful tonnage is a late-2020s proposition. TRISO output is also stacked on top of the HALEU bottleneck: TRISO-X kernels require HALEU feed, so fabrication capacity cannot outrun enrichment capacity. Additional constraints are UCO kernel and coating throughput, the small qualified supplier base for high-purity graphite matrix and coating precursors, and the absence of a second commercial-scale Western line if TF3 slips.

li7.status: The most concentrated single-point dependency in the advanced nuclear fuel chain, and the least resolved. Russia and China are the only countries actively producing separated lithium-6 and lithium-7 at industrial scale, and that supply is not known to be available for nuclear development elsewhere; China is reported to source its own material from Russia. Western users of Li-7 hydroxide for PWR primary coolant pH control depend on legacy stockpiles and intermittent imports. For molten salt reactors the position is worse, since FLiBe requires isotopically pure Li-7 in tonne quantities per core. DOE has begun allocating legacy enriched molten salt inventory (Natura Resources secured an allocation) as a bridge, and Kairos Power has re-established FLiBe production capability, but neither creates domestic enrichment capacity.
suppliers: Russia (COLEX-process production; the only established industrial-scale source)
China (industrial-scale production, reportedly Russian-sourced feed; not available to Western nuclear buyers)
US DOE legacy inventory (MSRE-era enriched salt, allocated to developers such as Natura Resources)
Hexium (US, AVLIS laser separation, ~$12m raised, pre-commercial)
Precision Periodic (US, DOE-grant-backed scalable Li-6/Li-7 enrichment, pre-commercial)
Molten Salt Solutions and Kairos Power (FLiBe salt production and purification, dependent on upstream Li-7 feed)
UK Atomic Energy Authority (rebuilding national lithium isotope separation capability)
li7.capacity_note: Current global PWR demand for Li-7 is roughly 1 tonne per year. Projected molten salt reactor demand is on the order of 250 tonnes per year once commercialised, with tens of tonnes required per reactor - a two-order-of-magnitude step change against a Western production base of essentially zero. COLEX remains the only process demonstrated at industrial scale, and it is mercury-based, which is why it has not been rebuilt in the West. Alternatives - electrochemical migration, laser isotope separation and crown ether extraction - are described as largely experimental and underfunded. Hexium's stated ambition is to substantially reduce foreign reliance within three to five years.
li7.bottleneck: No Western industrial-scale lithium isotope separation exists, and the only proven process is environmentally disqualified in the US and EU. That means every Western MSR programme is currently underwritten by a finite DOE legacy salt inventory plus geopolitically adversarial imports. EPRI has framed the near-term Western response as conserve, recover and replace (Li-7 recycling from spent coolant and substitution) rather than new supply, which is a mitigation, not a fix. Realistic Western Li-7 production at MSR-relevant tonnage is late-2020s at the earliest and unfunded at scale.

metallic_fuel.status: Pre-commercial. No Western commercial-scale metallic HALEU fuel fabrication line is operating in 2026. Oklo's fuel fabrication facility at Idaho National Laboratory received DOE design concept approval and is intended to recover and recast EBR-II fuel for the Aurora powerhouse, which is the reason Oklo's first unit is decoupled from fresh HALEU supply. TerraPower's sodium-cooled Natrium received the first NRC construction permit for a commercial non-light-water reactor in March 2026, with its metallic fuel supply chain still being stood up. DOE announced in March 2026 an initiative to produce mixed oxide fuel at Savannah River to boost HALEU supplies, indicating that federal material recovery remains part of the near-term answer. Aalo Atomics and other microreactor developers are at the design and pilot stage.
suppliers: US DOE / Idaho National Laboratory Materials and Fuels Complex (pilot and recovery scale; EBR-II fuel recovery)
Oklo (dedicated fuel fabrication facility at INL, design concept approved by DOE)
TerraPower with Global Nuclear Fuel (Natrium metallic fuel supply chain in development)
BWX Technologies (specialty fuels and metallic fuel capability)
Framatome and Westinghouse (advanced fuel lines, primarily oxide today)
Aalo Atomics and other microreactor developers (design/pilot stage)
metallic_fuel.capacity_note: Output today is measured in laboratory and demonstration quantities, not tonnes. All credible near-term metallic fuel volumes derive either from recovered EBR-II inventory held by DOE or from downblended surplus HEU, both of which are finite federal stocks rather than commercial supply. Commercial-scale metallic HALEU fabrication is dependent on the Centrus and General Matter enrichment ramps described above and is realistically a 2029-2032 proposition.
metallic_fuel.bottleneck: Three compounding constraints: no licensed commercial metallic HALEU fabrication line exists, so every fast reactor first core depends on DOE facilities or DOE-held material; the NRC Category II licensing pathway for such a facility takes years (TRISO-X, the first to complete it, took from 2022 to February 2026); and metallic fuel casting at HALEU enrichment carries criticality-safety and pyrophoricity constraints that limit batch sizes and throughput. Fuel qualification data for high-burnup metallic HALEU fuel is also still being generated.

standard_leu_lwr.status: Mature and functioning, but structurally tight through the late 2020s as the West replaces Russian SWU. Urenco and Orano are the Western enrichment base, with Urenco USA the only commercially operating enricher in the United States. The US Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act of 2024 bans Russian LEU imports, with waivers available only through 2027 and a full prohibition thereafter, which is the single largest driver of the current expansion wave. Conversion, fabrication and VVER-compatible fuel qualification (Westinghouse and Framatome supplying Ukraine, Bulgaria, Czechia, Slovakia and Finland) are all functioning.
suppliers: Urenco (Capenhurst UK, Almelo Netherlands, Gronau Germany, Eunice USA)
Orano (Georges Besse II, Tricastin, France; Project Ike planned at Oak Ridge, Tennessee)
Centrus Energy (LEU and HALEU, Piketon; also an SWU broker)
Global Laser Enrichment / SILEX (Paducah, development stage)
Rosatom/TVEL and CNNC (excluded or being excluded from Western markets)
Westinghouse, Framatome, GNF, ENUSA, Kepco NF (fuel fabrication)
standard_leu_lwr.capacity_note: Urenco USA Eunice reached about 4,650 tSWU/y with its first expansion phase started up in May 2025, targeting 5,000 tSWU/y in 2026-27 and a further roughly 2,100 tSWU/y increment toward about 7,100 tSWU/y; Urenco announced a further significant US expansion in 2026. Urenco Almelo is going from about 5,100 to about 6,600 tSWU/y by 2030 and Gronau from 3,400 to 3,700 tSWU/y in 2026-27. Orano is expanding Georges Besse II by more than 30% (about 2.5 million SWU, from 7,500 to 10,000 tSWU/y) with production from 2028, and its $900m-backed Project Ike at Oak Ridge is specified at 7,400 tSWU/y with an NRC licence submission in early 2026 and production from 2031.
standard_leu_lwr.bottleneck: Timing, not technology. Every announced Western SWU increment lands between 2028 and 2031, while Russian supply is contractually curtailed from 2028, creating a squeeze window in the late 2020s. Conversion (UF6) capacity is the tighter upstream link than enrichment itself, and long-lead centrifuge manufacturing and cascade hall construction limit how fast capacity can be pulled forward. For newcomer markets the practical constraint is fabrication qualification and licensing rather than SWU availability.

transport_packaging.status: Partially solved for fresh fuel, unsolved at fleet scale and unsolved for irradiated HALEU. Certified or approved today: the DN30-X for enriched UF6 up to 20%, licensed by the NRC in March 2023, with criticality control via neutron-poison rods and DN30-10/DN30-20 variants optimised by enrichment level; the VP-55 Versa-Pac for uranium oxides, uranium metal and TRISO fuel up to 20% enrichment (up to about 2,880 kg UO2 per ISO container); the BU-D, internationally licensed with a 90 kg content limit and up to 70 units per ISO container; and NAC International's OPTIMUS-L, which received NRC approval to transport HALEU TRISO contents. The standard 30B cylinder is limited to 5% and is being evaluated for higher enrichment without DN30-X modifications. The TN Eagle modular cask is in development for higher-enrichment used fuel but is not licensed for HALEU. In December 2025 DOE awarded a combined $11m to five companies - NAC International (in both topic areas), Westinghouse, Container Technologies Industries, American Centrifuge Operating and Paragon D&E - under the HALEU Availability Program, split between new NRC-licensable package designs (up to three-year projects) and modification of existing designs for NRC certification (up to two-year projects).
transport_packaging.bottleneck: Two distinct problems. First, fleet quantity: the certified packages that do exist are low-capacity and exist in small numbers, so building enough units to move commercial-scale HALEU is the binding constraint even where a design is approved, and DOE's own programme is only now funding two-to-three-year design and certification efforts. Second, and harder, used fuel: current commercial used-fuel packages are only licensed to a maximum of 5% initial enrichment, so there is no certified route to move irradiated HALEU or irradiated TRISO off site at scale. That means an advanced reactor can be fuelled before there is a licensed way to remove its spent fuel, pushing operators toward extended at-reactor storage. Certification lead times of roughly three to five years plus fabrication mean this gap persists into the late 2020s. A third, softer constraint is international: NRC certification does not automatically confer validation by foreign competent authorities, so cross-border shipment to newcomer markets requires parallel approvals (the DN30-X required separate French licensing).
transport_packaging.note: For a siting screening tool the practical implication is that transport packaging, not enrichment tonnage, is often the first hard gate on delivering >5% enriched or TRISO fuel to a given country - and the gate is tighter on the return leg (irradiated fuel) than the delivery leg. Any country without an existing certified-package logistics route and a competent authority able to validate foreign package certificates should be scored down on deliverability independently of its policy stance.
